title: feat(tide): measure the metrics instead of inventing them
body:
feat(tide): measure the metrics instead of inventing them

Tide's metrics endpoint answered with one random number and three stale
ones:

    requestsPerSecond: Math.random() * 100,
    storageUsedGb: instance.storageUsedGb,   // written as 0 at provision
    objectCount: instance.objectCount,       // same

The random one is the obvious lie. The stale ones are worse, because they
look like readings: nothing in the codebase ever writes those two fields
again after provisioning, so every Tide instance ever created reported
"0.0 GB used, 0 objects" forever — and the storage bar on the detail page
drew "0.0% of storage capacity used" over a bucket that could be full.
The overview page summed the same fields into two headline tiles.

Follows lib/server/atlas/metrics.ts. Two sources, because the numbers
come from two different places: CPU, memory and disk belong to the
container and Proxmox already measures them; buckets, objects, bytes
stored and request rate belong to MinIO, and `mc admin info` is the
interface it offers. Every field is `number | null`, null means "not
measured", and an `unavailable` list names what could not be read and
why. The request rate is a rate somebody counted: two samples of
`minio_s3_requests_total` a second apart in one round trip, null when the
counter went backwards because MinIO restarted between them.

`mc` now installs at provision time. Both the credential path and this
one need it, and provision time is the moment the container is already
downloading from the internet — a binary download does not belong on a
read path polled every 30s.

Screens: the detail page renders "—" for null and an amber card listing
what was not measured. The list column and the two dashboard tiles that
summed never-updated fields now show configured quota and bucket count,
which is configuration the records actually know.

Three tests asserted the fabrication — one required all four fields to be
`number`, two required the storage numbers to echo the record. A test
that pins a fabrication is what keeps the fabrication alive; they now
assert the opposite, plus parser tests for both readings.

title: fix(provisioning): give the container the pool's own resolvers
body:
fix(provisioning): give the container the pool's own resolvers

Every Tide provision in production failed at the first line of its
install script:

    Failed to fetch http://deb.debian.org/debian/dists/trixie/InRelease
    Temporary failure resolving 'deb.debian.org'

The Mesh default pool is IPv6-only and carries the answer —
`nameservers: ["2606:4700:4700::1111", "2001:4860:4860::8888"]` — but the
provisioner passed `nameserver: process.env.DATA_PRODUCTS_NAMESERVER`, a
variable nobody sets. A guest with a static address has no DHCP to learn
DNS from, so it came up with no resolver at all, apt died, `set -e` took
the whole provision with it and the rollback deleted the container. The
failure looks like a network problem and is a missing line of config.

Spark, Email and Launch already had this fix (the #74 pattern), each with
its own copy of the same three functions. Tide, which had no copy, was
the one that was broken. So the fix is not a fourth copy: the helpers
move to `data-products/dns.ts` and the three existing copies now import
them, which is 60 lines less duplication and, more to the point, means
the next provisioner inherits the fix instead of rediscovering it.

Tide now passes `poolNameserver(pool)` to the container and prefixes its
apt work with the resolver write plus the bounded wait for resolution —
a freshly started LXC can reach apt before its route and resolver are up,
which produces the identical message for a container that would have
worked ten seconds later.

Found by provisioning a real instance through the client path during the
block A smoke, not by a test. Tests cover the resolver choice; nothing
short of a real container would have surfaced this.

The kickoff records it, plus a second smoke finding left uncorrected:
Flux reads `DATA_PRODUCTS_DEFAULT_NODE` for its default node while Tide
and Nexus read `PROXMOX_DEFAULT_NODE`. Only the latter is set in
production, so Flux provisions against "pve", a node that does not exist,
and times out. One line to fix, but it is the owner's call.

why. The request rate is a rate somebody counted: two samples of

counter went backwards because MinIO restarted between them.

one need it, and provision time is the moment the container is already

read path polled every 30s.

Nexus's metrics endpoint answered with three random numbers and a status
echo:

    readOpsPerSec:  Math.round(Math.random() * 8000 + 500),
    writeOpsPerSec: Math.round(Math.random() * 4000 + 200),
    latencyMs:      Math.round(Math.random() * 5 + 1),
    nodeHealthy:    cluster.status === "active",

A cluster with no keyspace of its own reported thousands of operations
per second. `nodeHealthy` is the worse one: it was never a health check,
it was the store's own status field read back, so a node that died an
hour ago stayed "Healthy" on screen until somebody edited the record.

ScyllaDB is now measured with `nodetool`, following
lib/server/atlas/metrics.ts: the container from Proxmox, and the ring
from `nodetool status` plus two `nodetool tablestats` samples a second
apart for the operation rates. Only non-system keyspaces count as this
cluster's traffic — counting system_schema would have an untouched
cluster reporting a steady trickle — and only the keyspace-level totals,
since the per-table blocks below them would double every number. Latency
is the count-weighted mean across those keyspaces, and nodetool's
"NaN ms" for a latency with no samples behind it is null, not zero.

30 seconds for that round trip rather than the 15 the other products use:
nodetool is a JVM tool run three times through `docker exec`, so it is
genuinely slower than a psql or a curl.

FerretDB refuses with NOT_IMPLEMENTED. It runs with `--handler=sqlite`,
which keeps no server statistics at all — no serverStatus, no counters,
nothing that could answer how many reads it has served. The screen reads
the same list and shows the reason instead of polling an endpoint that
answers 501 every thirty seconds.

The shape changed with the source: `latencyMs` becomes read and write
latency, and `nodeState` carries what nodetool actually said (UN, DN, UJ)
beside the boolean, which is now null when nobody could ask.

that required nodeHealthy to follow the record. They now assert the
refusal, the CONFLICT for a record with no container, the nulls and the

title: docs: port-forward withdrawal has never worked, and item 1 said otherwise (#135)
body:
docs: port-forward withdrawal has never worked, and item 1 said otherwise (#135)

Found by doing what the owner insisted on — provisioning real resources
instead of seeding rows, then destroying them and looking at what was left.

Two Flux clusters, created and deleted through the product's own API, left
3 of 3 DNAT rules behind. The log says why:

  [port-forward] failed to withdraw 9404: bash: -c: line 2:
  syntax error near unexpected token `2'

deleteDnatCommand generates `for _ in $(seq 1 10); do ... done`, and
nodeTarget.exec builds the ssh line with JSON.stringify — double quotes.
The local shell expands $(seq 1 10) before ssh runs, seq's newlines survive
inside the quotes, and the remote bash receives `for _ in 1⏎2⏎3…`. The
publish path has no $(...), which is why adding works and withdrawing
never has.

This corrects the item 1 survey, which attributed the 91 orphaned rules to
containers destroyed by hand outside the API. That is when they appeared;
it is not the whole mechanism. Deleting through the API leaks too, on every
deletion, and removePortForward is called without await with its {ok:false}
inspected by nobody.

The same run caught the publish side racing for /run/xtables.lock and
losing — while the cluster was still marked active advertising the endpoint
whose rule had just failed to appear. The 15-minute reconciler put it there
later, which is the reconciler doing its job, but by accident rather than
by anyone checking.

Also registered, all verified in production and then cleaned up:

  - Item 4 is worse on screen than on paper. A Flux cluster ninety seconds
    old, with zero topics and no possible connection, reported 3,223
    messages/sec and 498.8 KB/s.
  - The Atlas list screen is honest — it badges synthesized clusters
    DISCOVERED. The trap is for whoever reads the count, not the screen.
    The kickoff implied otherwise.
  - 112 of 112 dashboard routes answer 200.
  - Item 3's credential work proved end to end against real engines: the
    password Atlas issues authenticates against the real Postgres and a
    wrong one does not; same for RabbitMQ.
  - An Atlas credential cannot connect until a firewall rule admits it, and
    the only rule on the live cluster is an IPv4 /32 on an IPv6-only
    container.
  - Validating a screen means provisioning the resource, not seeding a row.
    Seeding manufactures exactly the phantom state this codebase is prone
    to — the owner's correction, and it is right.

spawn("/bin/sh", ["-c", …]). Inside double quotes the LOCAL shell expands
$(...), ${...} and backticks before ssh runs, and a real newline becomes a
literal backslash-n. deleteDnatCommand emitted `for _ in $(seq 1 10)`, the
local shell turned that into ten newline-separated numbers still inside the
quotes, and the remote bash got `for _ in 1⏎2⏎3…`. Nothing was ever
withdrawn. shq() single-quotes instead, and its test runs each string
through a real /bin/sh and compares byte for byte — including the case that
names the defect: JSON.stringify turns `echo $((6*7))` into `echo 42`.

THE COMMAND. Fixing the transport is not enough, because a command that
works only because the transport is right is a trap for the next person.
The iptables commands now contain no `$` at all — the pass counter is a
literal word list — with a test that fails if `$(` or a backtick returns.

THE CALLERS. removePortForward was called fire-and-forget from nine places,
so a rejection became an unhandled one and {ok:false} was inspected by
nobody. They now await withdrawForward, which names the owner and logs
LEAKED <port> for <owner> when it fails. It deliberately does not throw:
one stuck rule must not abort the rest of a teardown.

Also: every iptables call takes -w 5. The same production run caught the
publish side losing /run/xtables.lock to Docker on node-1 while the cluster
was marked active advertising the endpoint whose rule had just failed to
appear. Waiting for the lock is half that fix; nobody checking the publish
result before marking active is the other half, and it is still open.

This corrects docs/dnat-state-reconciliation.md, which attributed the 91
orphaned rules to containers destroyed by hand outside the API. That is
when they appeared, not the mechanism. Both docs now say plainly that this
stops NEW orphans and does not remove the 91 — that is still the cleanup
script, and still the owner's call.

Verified: 66 network tests and 13 quoting tests pass; typecheck unchanged;
full suite 20 failed files against a 19 baseline, and the extra
(tests/blaze/04-lifecycle) passes in isolation — it is order-dependent like
tests/ignite/03 and tests/herald/04, on a machine that had 26 vitest
workers competing at the time.

title: refactor: nothing in the product is mocked, and Settings actually settles things (#143)
body:
refactor: nothing in the product is mocked, and Settings actually settles things (#143)

* refactor: nothing in the product is mocked any more

The owner's call, after Pulse was caught serving six invented services as
live telemetry: no mock datasources in the product at all. Four existed.

RADAR was the one that mattered and shipped separately (#141): query()
swallowed every ClickHouse failure and returned [], so an unreachable
backend rendered as a healthy cluster with zero nodes.

HARBOR had the same defect, latent. `listRepositories` turned an
unreachable registry into an empty catalogue — an operator could read that
as their images being gone. Worse, `getRepository` could not tell "no tags"
from "the request failed", because listTagNames returned [] for both, and
the catalog check meant to disambiguate failed silently too: the method
returned a repository object with zero tags for a name that might not
exist. listTagNames now returns null on failure and both paths throw
HarborBackendUnavailableError, which the route answers as 503. getOverview
keeps returning a value, because it already has a health field to say
"unreachable" with — and now also "degraded", when the catalog answered but
a tag listing did not.

LAUNCH shipped a mock as the DEFAULT while its own comment still said the
real datasource "lands in PR 2". PR 2 landed; the default never changed, so
anyone without LAUNCH_DATASOURCE=real got two invented services. Production
sets it. A fresh clone did not.

PULSE's mock was made opt-in in #138 and is now deleted outright, along
with the PULSE_DATASOURCE=mock branch that bought it.

Test doubles are untouched and stay: launch.test's fakeHarbor is injected
into the function under test, and the Launch route test now stubs the
datasource instead of asserting the deleted mock's contents. An injected
double is a test tool; a mock wired in as the product default is what this
removes. The two describe blocks that tested the mocks' own in-memory
behaviour went with them — that was never product behaviour.

RADAR_STRICT_REAL and HARBOR_DATASOURCE go too. A flag that selects between
truth and fiction is a flag that can be set wrong.

* feat(settings): make the display preferences actually be preferences

Both dropdowns on the Settings screen were bare `<select>` elements — no
onChange, no value, no state, just `<option selected>`. Polling Interval
showed "15 seconds" while the QueryClient refetched every 30, and choosing
another number did nothing: not for the session, not after a reload. Theme
was inert too, sitting a few pixels from a header toggle that had worked
all along.

A control that looks like it works and does not is worse than no control,
because the failure reads as "it didn't take this time" rather than "this
has never done anything". Same family as everything else this session
removed, wearing the clothes of a settings screen.

Polling now lives in a persisted zustand store and Providers applies it to
the live QueryClient, so a change takes effect without a reload and
survives one. The default is 30s — what the client actually did — not the
15 the screen claimed. A rehydrated value is validated against the offered
options before it becomes the refetch interval for every query in the app:
localStorage is editable by anyone at the keyboard, and a value from an
older build can outlive the build.

Theme is wired to next-themes, which already owned it. The select is a
second door onto that state, not a second copy of it — the header toggle
and this dropdown now move together.

About said "Proxmox Manager / 1.0.0-beta" as hardcoded strings, on an app
branded SideFuel Cloud at package version 0.1.0, with a GitHub link to a
repository that does not exist. The version is read from package.json now.

useEffect+setState pair, which trips react-hooks/set-state-in-effect —

fix(devices): o force do reparo era descartado antes de sair do painel (#713)

Device Baileys em status terminal (`logged_out`, `banned`) é irrecuperável
pela tela. O BB devolve a receita na própria mensagem de erro — "re-pair
explicitly (connect with force=true...)" — e o front JÁ mandava `force: true`
(whatsappDevicesApi.ts:396, de duas telas). O flag morria no meio:

  front            manda { force: true }                    ok
  controller       sem @Body -> ValidationPipe descarta      200, em silêncio
  service          client.reconnectDevice(bbDeviceId)        sem force

Ou seja, o reparo existia ponta a ponta menos no único hop que importava. O
usuário sem saída apagava o device e criava outro — que foi o que aconteceu
em staging em 17/08.

O contrato do outro lado está íntegro e foi conferido no building-blocks-v2:
device.router.ts:255 `if (body.force)` -> wpp-queue.service.ts:136
`{ force: 'true' }` -> wpp-consumer.ts:880 `{ repair: force === 'true' }` ->
`isTerminal && repair` -> wipeAuthState -> registro novo.

O @Transform devolvendo o valor cru no DTO não é redundante com o
@IsBoolean(): o pipe roda com enableImplicitConversion, que converteria a
string "false" em true (string não vazia) e dispararia um reparo destrutivo
que ninguém pediu. Medido: sem ele o teste recebia 201 em vez de 400.

`force` só viaja quando alguém pediu. Nada de { force: false } por padrão —

body:
fix(billing): soluço do BB jogava assinante no assistente de configuração

O `catch` de `GET /billing/status` dizia "fail open" e fazia o oposto:
deixava `hasSubscription` em `false`, o que vira
`setupRequired: 'subscription'` — e o front (`App.tsx`) substitui o painel
INTEIRO pelo `FullScreenSetupWizard`.

Ou seja: um timeout do BB tirava do ar todas as telas de quem já é
assinante. A saída visível para o usuário era escolher um plano de novo,
que "resolvia" até o próximo soluço. Foi assim que o sintoma chegou
("tenho que escolher free toda vez").

A correção é distinguir dois estados que o `false` sozinho não separa:

- o BB RESPONDEU que não há assinatura  → exige configuração;
- o BB NÃO respondeu                     → segue funcionando.

O segundo agora sai como `subscriptionUnknown: true`, para a tela poder
dizer "não deu para confirmar" em vez de afirmar que não há assinatura.

`getStatus` não tinha teste NENHUM — por isso o defeito viveu num
endpoint que decide se o produto inteiro abre. Vão seis, cobrindo os
quatro degraus (organização, conta, assinatura, faturamento desligado).
O teste do soluço foi verificado ao contrário: com o defeito de volta ele
falha; com a correção, passa.

* fix(security): tools de IA fail-closed — sai o token global compartilhado (E-2)

E-2 era o último CRITICAL em aberto: 27 ferramentas de IA falando com o BB por
um `CATALISA_API_TOKEN` único e global. Quem não tivesse credencial própria
escrevia — e LIA — sob a organização compartilhada.

Não era teórico. Medido em produção antes de mexer:

    datastore.collections   19 coleções, 889 documentos
    18 das 19               sob b0000000-…-0001, a org default
    última escrita          2026-07-20
    tenants                 12 raiz, 2 com credencial wpp-bb

A auditoria classificou isto como "arquitetural, não fazer no susto". Medindo,
não é: a encanação já tinha sido feita no plano de 12/07. Os 47 call sites de
`makeCatalisaRequest` JÁ passam o `userId`, e todo chamador real (assistente,
stream, plan-mode, agentes, orquestrado) preenche `context.userId`. Sub-usuário
também não quebra — `findAll` resolve por `getRootMasterId`, então herda a
credencial do master. Faltava só remover o fallback.

Some também o `try/catch` que engolia a falha de resolução num `logger.warn` e
caía no token compartilhado. Era o pior dos três casos: o tenant TINHA
credencial, saía pela global mesmo assim, e ninguém via. Credencial que não
resolve agora derruba a chamada.

A env var CONTINUA existindo — `billing-client`, `payments-client` e
`base-catalisa.handler` a consomem, com cadeias próprias. O que não pode voltar
é ela ser lida aqui, e há um teste fixando isso.

A mensagem de erro aponta a saída: o painel emite a chave sozinho pelo botão
"Gerar Automaticamente" (`POST /credentials/generate-bb-key`), sem segredo
vindo de fora.

O spec anterior documentava o fallback como correto — três dos seus quatro
testes afirmavam que cair no token global era o comportamento certo. Reescrito.
Sem o fix, 4 dos 6 testes novos falham.

IRMÃO AINDA ABERTO (E-2b): os workflow actions Catalisa
(`base-catalisa.handler.getApiToken`) mantêm o mesmo fallback quando a config

title: docs: the smoke found a third wall, and it is not code
body:
docs: the smoke found a third wall, and it is not code

The DNS fix (#151) worked in production: `apt-get update` now passes and
the Tide install runs on to the MinIO download, where it hits a different
wall.

    curl: (7) Failed to connect to dl.min.io port 443 after 2 ms:
          Could not connect to server

Two milliseconds is network-unreachable, not a timeout. Checked on the
host, `dl.min.io` is the one vendor host the platform downloads from that
has no AAAA record — deb.debian.org, github.com, registry-1.docker.io and
get.stalw.art all have real IPv6. Every Mesh pool here is IPv6-only, so a
Tide container cannot reach the only place it fetches MinIO from.

No code change reaches that host. It is mirror the binary somewhere
IPv6-reachable (Harbor is right there and this would be its first real
use), give the pool NAT64/DNS64, or install MinIO from somewhere else —
all owner decisions, so this is registered as C3 rather than attempted.

Also recorded: the trap that made this hard to see. `getent ahostsv6`
answers with an IPv4-mapped address (`::ffff:…`) when there is no AAAA at
all, which reads as "it has IPv6" to anyone skimming. The prefix is the
tell.

title: fix(provisioning): give the container the pool's own resolvers (#151)
body:
fix(provisioning): give the container the pool's own resolvers (#151)

Every Tide provision in production failed at the first line of its
install script:

    Failed to fetch http://deb.debian.org/debian/dists/trixie/InRelease
    Temporary failure resolving 'deb.debian.org'

The Mesh default pool is IPv6-only and carries the answer —
`nameservers: ["2606:4700:4700::1111", "2001:4860:4860::8888"]` — but the
provisioner passed `nameserver: process.env.DATA_PRODUCTS_NAMESERVER`, a
variable nobody sets. A guest with a static address has no DHCP to learn
DNS from, so it came up with no resolver at all, apt died, `set -e` took
the whole provision with it and the rollback deleted the container. The
failure looks like a network problem and is a missing line of config.

Spark, Email and Launch already had this fix (the #74 pattern), each with
its own copy of the same three functions. Tide, which had no copy, was
the one that was broken. So the fix is not a fourth copy: the helpers
move to `data-products/dns.ts` and the three existing copies now import
them, which is 60 lines less duplication and, more to the point, means
the next provisioner inherits the fix instead of rediscovering it.

Tide now passes `poolNameserver(pool)` to the container and prefixes its
apt work with the resolver write plus the bounded wait for resolution —
a freshly started LXC can reach apt before its route and resolver are up,
which produces the identical message for a container that would have
worked ten seconds later.

Found by provisioning a real instance through the client path during the
block A smoke, not by a test. Tests cover the resolver choice; nothing
short of a real container would have surfaced this.

The kickoff records it, plus a second smoke finding left uncorrected:
Flux reads `DATA_PRODUCTS_DEFAULT_NODE` for its default node while Tide
and Nexus read `PROXMOX_DEFAULT_NODE`. Only the latter is set in
production, so Flux provisions against "pve", a node that does not exist,
and times out. One line to fix, but it is the owner's call.

body:
feat(capture-links): o lead capturado nasce dentro do funil

Link de captura É topo de funil, e mesmo assim o lead que chegava por ele
nascia FORA de qualquer funil: `submitLead` criava o lead com tipo e
responsável, sem estágio nenhum. Ele aparecia na lista e nunca no quadro, e
`STAGE_ENTERED` não contava a entrada — a meta ficava menor que a
realidade, sem erro em log nenhum.

É o mesmo buraco que o formulário manual tinha, num lugar pior: aqui é a
porta da frente, por onde entra quem veio de campanha.

- `CaptureLink.stageId` (nullable, FK com `SetNull`): apagar um estágio não
  invalida o link, ele volta a capturar sem funil — o comportamento antigo.
- `create`/`update` aceitam e validam o estágio POR DONO (INV-4): id vindo
  do corpo é aceito por PERTENCER, não por existir. Sem isso um link
  poderia despejar leads no funil de outro tenant.
- `submitLead` repassa o estágio ao `LeadsService.create`, que valida,
  espelha o `status` da categoria e grava a transição de entrada.
- Formulário ganha **Funil de destino** + **Estágio de entrada**, com a

title: fix(ai-assistant): elimina "Connection lost" e "sessão não existe" no chat (#730)
body:
fix(ai-assistant): elimina "Connection lost" e "sessão não existe" no chat (#730)

O painel-cliente-api roda com 2 réplicas e o estado do streaming (requestId +
streamToken) vive na MEMÓRIA do processo que atendeu o /ai/chat/start. O Traefik
já emite um cookie de sticky session (painel_api_srv) para prender o cliente
naquela réplica, mas o browser só manda cookie cross-origin com withCredentials
— e nem o POST /start nem o EventSource pediam credenciais. Resultado: o SSE
caía numa réplica aleatória.

MEDIDO em produção: 10 requisições sem cookie → 5 numa réplica, 5 na outra.
Round-robin exato, ou seja ~50% das mensagens do assistente morriam em 401 e
viravam "Connection lost. Please try again.". Com o cookie: 10/10 na mesma
réplica.

Correções:

- front: withCredentials no POST /ai/chat/start (para o browser GRAVAR o
  cookie), no EventSource (para ENVIÁ-LO) e no /ai/chat/cancel, que também
  procura a request em memória.
- back: o streamToken deixa de ser consumido na primeira validação. O
  EventSource reconecta sozinho e reapresenta o mesmo token; consumi-lo fazia
  toda reconexão virar 401 com a request ainda viva. O token segue aleatório
  (256 bits) e presa a um único requestId, e agora é descartado junto com a
  request.
- back: heartbeat SSE a cada 15s. Um turno passa minutos em loop de tools sem
  emitir nada, e o proxy derrubava a conexão por idle.
- front: onerror deixa de tratar reconexão transitória (readyState CONNECTING)
  como falha fatal, e não mostra erro se o turno já tinha completado.
- back: sessionId obsoleto do localStorage passa a abrir uma sessão nova em vez
  de estourar 404 "Session <id> not found" no meio da conversa.

title: feat(leads): dizer a que funil o lead pertence, pela tela
body:
feat(leads): dizer a que funil o lead pertence, pela tela

Você perguntou onde fica o mecanismo de vincular lead a funil. Ele existia
em dois lugares, e nenhum dos dois era alcançável por um formulário.

**Por lead** o vínculo é `Lead.stageId` → estágio → funil. O
`UpdateLeadDto` já aceitava `stageId`, mas o formulário do lead nunca teve
esse campo: tinha Nome, Email, Telefone, Tipo, Status e Notas. A única
forma de dizer o funil era ir ao Kanban e ARRASTAR o cartão. Quem editasse
pela lista não tinha como.

E o `CreateLeadDto` nem aceitava `stageId` — todo lead criado pela tela
nascia FORA de qualquer funil, com `status` preenchido e estágio nulo. O
`status` é ESPELHO de `stage.category`; o espelho sem o objeto é o que
fazia o quadro começar vazio com a lista cheia.

**Por tipo de lead** existe `LeadType.pipelineId`, com comentário e tudo no
schema — e o DTO do servidor não o declarava. Com `whitelist: true`,
mandá-lo era descartado em silêncio e a API respondia 200. Só o instalador
de pacote de vertical conseguia gravá-lo, escrevendo direto pelo Prisma. E
ninguém em `modules/leads/` o lia para decidir coisa alguma.

Agora:

- formulário do lead ganha **Funil** e **Estágio**, com cascata (trocar o
  funil limpa o estágio, senão sobra um par que não existe);
- `CreateLeadDto` aceita `stageId`, e o serviço faz as três coisas que
  andam juntas: valida o estágio POR DONO, espelha o `status` a partir de
  `stage.category`, e grava a transição de entrada na MESMA transação
  (INV-5) — sem ela, `STAGE_ENTERED` não conta quem já nasce no funil e a
  meta fica menor que a realidade;
- tipo de lead ganha **Funil padrão**, que SUGERE: escolher o tipo
  pré-seleciona o funil no formulário do lead, e quem cria pode trocar.
  Sem isso o campo seria enfeite, que é o defeito que ele veio corrigir.

Um lead segue em NO MÁXIMO um funil: `stageId` é FK única e não há tabela
de junção. `LeadStageTransition` é histórico, não vínculo.

+5 testes: nascer no estágio, espelho do status, recusa de estágio de outro
dono, o caminho sem estágio não abrir transação, e `stageId: null`
sobreviver ao whitelist — é assim que "Fora de funil" tira o lead do funil.

title: fix(flux): a broker with no queues has no backlog, and says so
body:
fix(flux): a broker with no queues has no backlog, and says so

The first RabbitMQ cluster to reach `active` in production answered:

    "messagesPerSec": 0, "queueCount": 0, "connectionCount": 0,
    "messagesReady": null, "messagesUnacked": null,
    "unavailable": []

Two nulls with an empty `unavailable` puts "—" on screen with nothing
beside it explaining why — the exact "grid of dashes reads as nothing is
happening" failure this module was written to prevent, reintroduced by
its own parser.

RabbitMQ omits `queue_totals` entirely on a broker with no queues, the
same way it omits `message_stats` before anything is published. The
message_stats case was already read as zero and documented; this one was
read as unknown. A broker with no queues has nothing waiting in them:
that is a reading. When queues do exist and the totals are missing, it
stays null, because then it really is a gap.

And a net under all of it: if any field comes back unmeasured and nothing
in `unavailable` accounts for it, the response now says so rather than
leaving the screen to imply zero.

Found by provisioning a real cluster, not by a test — the suites only
ever saw an unreachable broker, where everything is null for one obvious
reason. The two new parser cases cover both shapes.

title: fix(web): stop seeding form state from effects (#170)
body:
fix(web): stop seeding form state from effects (#170)

Thirty-six `react-hooks/set-state-in-effect` errors across thirty-five files
were one mistake repeated: a dialog or page would declare its fields with empty
`useState` defaults, then run an effect whose only job was to overwrite them
with the props or query data the component already had. The effect was doing
work React does for free.

The cost is a wasted render, and it is not invisible. React renders once with
the empty defaults, commits that to the DOM, runs the effect, and renders again
with the real values. Every edit dialog in this app therefore painted blank
inputs before showing the record you clicked on. Where the seeding effect
listed a query result in its dependencies, the cascade was worse than cosmetic:
the query client refetches on a thirty second interval, so a background refetch
re-ran the effect and silently discarded whatever the operator had typed into
an unsaved firewall rule or SDN zone.

Three techniques replace it, chosen per case rather than applied uniformly.
Most dialogs now split into a shell that owns the chrome and a form component
rendered inside `DialogContent`; Radix unmounts that subtree on close, so React
re-runs the `useState` initialisers on the next open and the reset branch of
the old effect disappears. A `key` on the form covers the remaining job, which
is re-seeding when the dialog is repointed at a different record while still
open. Values that were only ever derived from other state, such as the Mesh
child-prefix clamp and the default domain in the email pages, are now computed
during render and stored nowhere. Genuinely external state reads its own source
directly through `useSyncExternalStore`: the viewport query in `SplitView` and
the localStorage-backed onboarding checklist, which was keeping a copy of
localStorage in React state and filling the copy from an effect.

Two effects turned out to be dead. Both member-dialog tabs render inside
`DialogContent` and cleared themselves when `open` went false, which could only
ever happen during the closing animation, blanking the form as it faded out.

Behaviour is preserved deliberately, including behaviour that is arguably
wrong. The migrate dialog's defaults were chosen once per open and never
revised, an intent its `eslint-disable-line` made explicit, so its form is
mounted without a key to keep exactly that. Atlas consumes its one-shot
`?create=true` on close now rather than on open, because stripping the param
while the dialog was up would flip the key underneath it.

title: fix(atlas): revoke on the engine, reject in pg_hba, and delete what a failed provision made
body:
fix(atlas): revoke on the engine, reject in pg_hba, and delete what a failed provision made

Three things Atlas claimed and did not do.

Revoking a credential wrote a tombstone in the store and nothing else. The
row left the screen, the audit trail recorded that access had been withdrawn,
and the Postgres role kept its LOGIN attribute and every grant it was issued
with — so whoever held the password carried on connecting and reading data
indefinitely, with the platform reporting the opposite. Revocation now runs
ALTER ROLE ... NOLOGIN inside the primary container as the postgres
superuser, over the same path issuance uses. NOLOGIN rather than DROP ROLE
because DROP fails whenever the role owns an object or holds a grant, which
issuance guarantees by granting ALL PRIVILEGES on the database, and reassigning
ownership is a decision about someone's data that this endpoint cannot make.
A revocation that commonly fails is a revocation that commonly leaves the
access running.

NOLOGIN only stops the next connection, so the open sessions are terminated
too: the connections that matter here are pooled and live for days, and
without pg_terminate_backend "revoked" would mean "revoked whenever some
unrelated process happens to restart". The order is NOLOGIN first and the
kill second — reversed, the pooler reconnects within milliseconds and the
whole thing looks like it worked.

If either statement fails, the call returns DEPENDENCY_UNAVAILABLE and writes
nothing: no tombstone, no audit event. That is the rule credentialWiringFailed
already applies on the way in, and it exists because a store that claims a
withdrawal the engine never performed is worse than an error — nobody goes
looking for access they were told was already gone. The role name is derived
by one shared helper now, since issuance writes CREATE USER unquoted and
Postgres folds it to lower case; deriving it twice is how revocation would
start missing.

A deny firewall rule was generated as `hostnossl ... scram-sha-256`, which
denies nothing. hostnossl narrows a line to clients not using SSL and the
line still ends in an auth method, so the blocked host only had to skip TLS
to be let in with its password. Denies are now the pg_hba `reject` method,
emitted in the operator's own order — pg_hba is first-match, and nothing
reorders by action because "allow this host, reject its range" and "reject
this host, allow its range" are both legitimate and differ only by order.
Since a deny can now actually lock someone out, assessCredentialAccess models
the one arrangement it can prove — a /0 reject in the clients' address family
above every allow — and stays silent on everything narrower rather than tell
someone their working firewall is broken.

An HA provision kept its vmids in a local array written to the store only at
the last step, so a replica that failed mid-loop left the row saying
[primary] while replica containers ran on the node, and the failure path
released the IPs and deleted nothing. Containers are recorded the moment they
exist, and the rollback deletes them, releasing each address only once its
container is confirmed gone — an address handed back while an LXC still
answers on it is a duplicate IP on the shared L2. A container that survives
the rollback stays on the row with its address reserved and is named on the
Herald event, because the row is the only thing deprovisioning has to find it
by. The rollback is skipped once the cluster is recorded live, so a failing
Herald emit can no longer cost a customer their database.

title: docs: the wave of six, and the three findings it surfaced (#165)
body:
docs: the wave of six, and the three findings it surfaced (#165)

Records what shipped on 2026-08-19 — the quota fix, the vmid retry, the
crypto ceiling, the conditional hook, the dead Settings links and Herald's
export refusal — and, more usefully, what running five agents over this
code turned up.

Two entries in this file were wrong and are corrected. "13
rules-of-hooks errors" read like thirteen tabs waiting to die; twelve were
a server-side predicate named usePostgres() that the linter treated as a
hook because of the prefix, and the real bug was one component. And
set-state-in-effect is 36 errors across 35 files rather than a footnote,
though they share a single shape, so it is one repeated pattern and not 35
problems.

Three new findings, all registered rather than fixed. Ignite and Blaze
write a SUCCESSFUL deprovision back as `failed` and have no terminal
status at all, so a deleted function is indistinguishable from a broken
one and holds its quota forever — and the typecheck error that has sat in
the baseline as noise is a test reaching for the `deleted` status that
does not exist, which makes it a symptom rather than dirt. Nine
provisioners still carry the vmid race, Atlas twice, where a multi-node
cluster can collide with itself. And Flux and Nexus never got updated when
addPortForward became awaitable, so a failed forward there is still
silently dropped.

title: fix(ignite): verify the publish, and stop the invoke test racing itself
body:
fix(ignite): verify the publish, and stop the invoke test racing itself

Ignite was the last provisioner calling `addPortForward` fire-and-forget. It
then marked the function `active`, stored its endpoint URL and emitted a
`success` event, with nothing having checked whether the host DNAT rule was
ever installed. `addPortForward` resolves `{ok:false}` instead of throwing —
that is how it reports a lost race for /run/xtables.lock against Docker — so
the catch block never saw it. The result was a green function handing out a
URL that refused every request: the tenant wires that URL into a webhook or a
cron and finds out hours later, from something missing downstream, that it
never worked. The forward is now awaited and its result read, the endpoint is
not stored when it did not publish, and the Herald event drops to `partial`
naming the port, the underlying error and the address the function would have
had.

Recording that outcome needed a status Ignite did not have, so this adds
`degraded` to FunctionStatus rather than reusing an existing member, and says
so plainly because it is a platform type change plus migration 0037. The
alternatives are all worse. `active` is the defect. `failed` is wrong twice
over: the provision did not die — the container is up and the runtime is
installed and serving on 8080 — and nothing transitions out of `failed`, so
the function would sit red forever holding the org's tier slot while its LXC
stayed on the node, and an operator reading "failed" reasonably rebuilds,
leaking the container that is still running. `deploying` would claim work is
in flight when nothing is running. `degraded` is what every other data
product already uses for exactly this state, and — the part that makes it
repair rather than merely honest — it is a live status for the port-forward
reconciler, which already carries an `ignite` descriptor on base 7000 → 8080
and collects Ignite functions. A function left degraded is picked up on the
next pass and its missing rule re-applied. The migration only ADDs the enum
value; no existing row is rewritten, because nothing here can tell a working
forward from a missing one. The badge renders it amber rather than red for
the same reason the reconciler matters, and the service's deletable states
gain it so a degraded function is not the one thing a tenant cannot remove.

The second half is a genuinely flaky test. tests/ignite/03-api-routes
registered `vi.mock` for the provisioner twice, and vi.mock on one path is
last-one-wins, so the second block silently replaced the first. The first
existed to keep background writes out of the store: every store write is a
read-modify-write of a single JSON file, so a write that began before a later
test created its function rewrites the file without it and that test answers
404. It achieved this by making `invokeFunction` never settle, which also
meant the invoke path was never exercised past "queued". The override made it
resolve and put the race straight back — the file failed 3 of 6 baseline
runs, always on `data.id starts with 'iginv-'`. There is now one mock that
resolves, and the three tests that trigger the fire-and-forget chain wait for
its tail — the function's invocationCount bump — before returning, which is a
real happens-after signal rather than a sleep. Ten consecutive runs pass.

One test mock had to move with the code: 08-terminal-status stubbed
`addPortForward` as resolving `undefined`, which was harmless while nobody
read the result and became a thrown TypeError once somebody did. It now
returns the real `{ok:true}` shape.

title: feat(tide): a way out for a container that only has IPv6 (#157)
body:
feat(tide): a way out for a container that only has IPv6 (#157)

Every Mesh pool here is IPv6-only, which is why a Tide container needs no
DNAT to be reached. It is also why it cannot reach `dl.min.io`, which has
no AAAA record, so MinIO could never be downloaded and no Tide instance
ever finished provisioning. The download failed in two milliseconds with
"Could not connect to server" — network-unreachable wearing a connection
error's clothes.

The container now keeps its public IPv6 on eth0 for inbound and gains a
private IPv4 on eth1 purely to get out. That costs no public address:
172.10.0.0/24 is RFC1918 and the host has masqueraded it out of its single
public IPv4 since this cluster existed —

    -A POSTROUTING -s 172.10.0.0/24 -o vmbr0 -j MASQUERADE

which is how every other guest installs packages. Two default routes, one
per address family, which do not compete.

`firewall=0` on the new NIC is not decoration. With firewall=1 Proxmox
builds an fwbr bridge in front of it and NAT egress breaks inside an
unprivileged LXC, with apt failing "Could not resolve host" — the exact
symptom this interface exists to remove. eth0 pins it for the same reason
and the test pins it here.

The address comes from `allocateLxcIp`, which scans every guest's every
NIC and throws rather than fall back to a scheme that cannot see what is
taken. That matters more than usual: vmbr1 is one L2 spanning both nodes,
so a duplicate is not a clash, it is a black hole for whoever loses the
ARP race.

Tide only. Spark installs over apt and Email uses a host with IPv6; both
work today and touching them would be risk without a defect. The helper is
shared so the next module that hits this wall inherits it.

NAT64/DNS64 at the gateway remains the larger, better answer — it fixes
this for every IPv6-only guest at once and needs no second NIC. It also
cannot help anything dialling a literal IPv4 address, since nothing asks
DNS then. This is the smaller, reversible move, and it comes out by
deleting one line if NAT64 lands.

title: docs: the C findings became fixes, and one new one took their place
body:
docs: the C findings became fixes, and one new one took their place

C10, C11 and C12 are closed by #173-#175. What is worth carrying forward
is not that they are closed but what closing them turned up.

Atlas revocation chose NOLOGIN over DROP ROLE because issuance grants the
role CREATE ON SCHEMA public, so the first object it creates makes DROP
fail — and a drop that commonly fails is a revocation that commonly
leaves the access running. Open sessions are terminated after the
NOLOGIN, not before, or the pooler reconnects and it merely looks like it
worked. On the way there: the store keeps the raw username while issuance
writes it unquoted, which Postgres folds to lower case, so without one
shared helper revocation would have altered a role that does not exist
and reported success against nothing.

The Courier decision is the one to remember. Adding it to
PRODUCT_DESCRIPTORS would have been inert rather than merely wrong:
collectForProduct pushes to unresolved and continues before extraForwards
is ever consulted, so the entry would sit in the list looking like
coverage while emitting zero rules. Port 4190, the live ManageSieve rule
that was one removeOrphans=true from deletion, now has an owner.

One new finding replaces them: the JSON store has no read-modify-write
atomicity, so concurrent writers lose updates. Production runs Postgres,
but the code default is json — the same shape as the crypto ceiling.

Three questions are left explicitly for the owner, including whether
MAIL_PORTS omitting 143 is deliberate.

title: fix(herald): export refuses instead of faking a completed download
body:
fix(herald): export refuses instead of faking a completed download

Herald's export was theatre from end to end. `POST /api/herald/export`
wrote an export job, a `setTimeout` moved it to `running` and then to
`completed` about two and a half seconds later, and the job it saved
carried a `downloadUrl` of `/api/herald/export/{id}/download` — a route
that has never existed in this codebase. The Events screen offered an
Export button, toasted "Export job created", and the status poll watched
the timer report success. A user who followed the link got a 404. No file
was ever written, anywhere, in any format.

Nothing about exporting is impossible here: the events are real, they are
queryable, and `GET /api/herald/events` already serialises them as JSON.
What was missing was a writer and a route to serve what it wrote. So this
takes the established answer for a capability that does not exist —
NOT_IMPLEMENTED with a message that says what is absent and what the
operator can do instead — rather than inventing an exporter.

The refusal is only half of it. An honest 501 behind an inviting button is
still a screen telling the user something untrue, so the fact lives in
`lib/data-products/herald-export-support.ts`, next to its siblings for
metrics and credentials, and the Events page reads the same module: the
button is gone and the reason stands in its place, naming the events API
as the way to get the data out today.

`HeraldExportJob` record, its status field, the timer, the store
collection, the polling hook and its query keys, the status endpoint that
could now only ever 404, and the input schema for an operation that will
not run. `herald_meta_export_jobs` is dropped in migration 0035 along with
its two enums — every row in it recorded a completion that did not happen,
and kept around it would read as export history.

title: fix(tide,spark,herald,atlas,courier): publish checks its result everywhere (#171)
body:
fix(tide,spark,herald,atlas,courier): publish checks its result everywhere (#171)

Flux and Nexus were taught to inspect the result of addPortForward before
marking a resource ready. The same defect was still live in Tide, Spark,
Herald and Courier, which fired the forward without awaiting it at all, and
in Atlas, which awaited it, read the result, and then console.errored and
marked the cluster active with its endpoint anyway. A log line on a server
nobody tails is not an operator-visible signal; from every seat that
matters it is indistinguishable from not checking.

All five now follow the shape set by the first pass. A failed publish makes
the resource degraded rather than active, the endpoint is not stored, and
the Herald event drops to partial carrying the port, the underlying error
and the address the resource would have had. Degraded rather than failed
because the container is up and the software installed — only a host NAT
rule is missing, every one of these failure paths rolls back by deleting
the container, and degraded is a live status for the port-forward
reconciler, so the rule comes back on the next pass and the resource
repairs in place. The endpoint is withheld because the detail pages render
their connection panels from the endpoint alone, without consulting status:
a stored endpoint is a published one as far as the customer is concerned.
Herald withholds lokiEndpoint on the same reasoning, and more urgently — a
log shipper pointed at a dead push URL drops silently, so the first sign of
trouble would be an empty log search hours later.

Courier is the case where degraded on its own says too little. It publishes
five well-known ports in a loop and they fail independently, and which one
is missing decides what happens next: 25 missing is an inbound outage
senders retry for days before bouncing, 587 missing is an outbound outage
the customer feels immediately, 993 missing means mail arrives and nobody
can read it, and 443 missing takes the Stalwart admin API with it. So each
missing port is named together with what stops working, the ports map
records only what actually published, and the event says plainly that no
reconciler covers Courier's forwards — they are fixed well-known numbers
rather than base+vmid and the reconciler walks only the seven products in
network/desired-state.ts, so promising an automatic repair would leave an
operator waiting for one that never comes.

Two consequences of recording a mail server as degraded had to be handled
alongside. ensureMailServer re-provisions a failed or deleting server from
scratch; degraded fell into that branch, which would have stood a second
container up beside a running Stalwart holding real mailboxes and leaked
the first one over a missing iptables rule, so a degraded server is now
returned as-is. And the two guards that gate mailbox and domain work on an
active server now accept degraded, because the admin API they use is
reached on the container's own address and no DNAT rule is involved —
refusing every remaining function of a working server because POP3 is
unreachable from the internet would be pure loss.

The verification test grows from Flux and Nexus to all seven. Stashing the
five provisioners and re-running turns the twelve new failure-path cases
red while all thirteen controls — every happy path, and the IPv6 pool where
there is no NAT to fail — stay green.

title: fix(network): give Nexus its real port and Courier a reconciler (#173)
body:
fix(network): give Nexus its real port and Courier a reconciler (#173)

The Nexus descriptor declared an internal port of 8081 and nothing has ever
listened on 8081 in a Nexus container: the provisioner installs ScyllaDB on
9042 or FerretDB on 27017, chosen by the cluster's engine. A wrong internal
port fails both halves of reconciliation at once, because the rule is
compared whole — the real 8000+vmid to 9042 rule has no owner and reads as
an orphan, while the "repair" appends a DNAT into a black hole that makes
the cluster look reconciled and forward to nothing. The descriptor now reads
the engine off the row, mirroring the provisioner's own branch including its
default: anything that is not scylladb is FerretDB there, so it is here too.

Courier had no coverage at all, so nothing re-applied its mail forwards
after a reboot or a lost xtables lock; they stayed gone until someone
noticed mail was not arriving. It does not fit ProductDescriptor and is not
made to: its external ports are fixed well-known numbers rather than
base+vmid, it stores no endpoint to derive a port from, and it publishes
seven forwards per server. Bending it into a descriptor is not merely ugly,
it is inert — portBase and internalPort returning null both make
collectForProduct report the instance unresolved and continue before
extraForwards is consulted, so the entry would sit in PRODUCT_DESCRIPTORS
looking like coverage and produce no rules. It gets its own collector
instead, beside the generic one, where the difference is readable. The port
list is imported from the mail config rather than copied, because a list
that drifts from what the provisioner opens is the exact failure this
coverage exists to prevent.

This does not touch removal, and it cannot cause one. toRemove is drawn only
from host rules that have no owner and fall inside 4000-9999; a desired
forward can only take a rule out of that set, never put one in, and rules on
a colliding port are excluded from removal as well. Six of Courier's seven
ports sit outside the managed range and stay invisible to deletion by
construction. The seventh, ManageSieve on 4190, is the live production rule
the state survey found sitting unowned one removeOrphans=true away from
deletion; it now has an owner while a live mail server row resolves, which
is a strict reduction in what removal would take. The range is deliberately
not widened to cover mail: adds are not fenced by range, so nothing would be
gained, while 25 and 443 would become deletable the moment the email store
looked empty. Ownership is conditional and the explicit port-and-destination
allowlist is still owed; the module comment says so rather than claiming the
hazard is closed.

The container IP is resolved live for Courier as it is for the data
products, and it matters more here: these are shared infrastructure port
numbers, so a rule built from a stale stored address would not fail quietly,
it would publish the host's port 25 and port 443 to whichever container
inherited that IP. An unresolvable container yields no forward and a report.

title: fix(atlas): audit credential issuance and say when it cannot connect
body:
fix(atlas): audit credential issuance and say when it cannot connect

Atlas emitted eleven kinds of Herald event and not one of them was about a
credential. Creating one issues a Postgres identity that can read customer
data; renaming a database left two entries in the trail, and issuing an
identity left none. Every sibling data product — Flux, Nexus, Spark, Tide —
already emits credential.created, so Atlas was the one product handing out
database access in silence.

Issuance and revocation now go down both trails, and they are not
redundant. Herald answers "what happened on this cluster" and feeds the
Events tab; the Aegis audit store is the identity trail — logins, IAM
changes, every Proxmox mutation with its policy decision — and is where
someone asks after an incident who was granted access to what. The actor is
the session that pressed the button, not the cluster's creator. Nothing on
either event can reconstruct the secret: who, which cluster, which database,
which username, and never the password, the hash, or a prefix of it. An
audit record for a credential has to be safe to keep forever and readable by
people who are not allowed to use the credential it describes.

The second half is the same problem wearing different clothes. Atlas
rebuilds pg_hba from atlas_firewall_rules, so a credential with no rule
admitting its origin is a user that exists and cannot connect. That
separation is deliberate — identity and network are two grants — but the
screen never said so, so the user got a working username and password that
failed at first use with "no pg_hba.conf entry for host", an error that
names the host and never mentions Atlas. Unaudited issuance and silent
access requirements are one defect: the platform knew something important
about a credential and told nobody. On the live cluster that shape is
already there — one IPv4 /32 on a container reachable only over IPv6, a rule
present, plausible and incapable of ever matching.

The verdict is computed from the live rule table by a client-safe function
the service and the screen both call, so the trail and the UI cannot drift
into different stories: the event records whether the credential was
admitted when it was issued, and the credential UI renders an amber notice
naming what is actually missing — no rules at all, rules scoped to other
roles, or rules in the wrong address family — with a button to the tab that
fixes it. It says nothing when a rule already admits the user, because a
permanent banner is wallpaper by the second week and wrong on every cluster
whose firewall is correct.

The audit store's path is now overridable, for the same reason every other
store's is: tests that record audit events must not append to the
developer's real one.

title: docs: deleting a resource does not give the quota back
body:
docs: deleting a resource does not give the quota back

Two findings from the 2026-08-19 smoke, both registered rather than
fixed.

C5, the serious one. Re-provisioning in the same org was refused with
TIER_LIMIT_EXCEEDED, "max: 2, current: 2" — and both clusters it counted
were `deleted`. Nexus, Atlas, Spark and Tide all count
`listClusters({ orgId })` with no status filter and hand `.length` to
checkTierLimit, and the soft delete keeps the row. So on the starter tier
a customer who creates and deletes two resources can never create a third:
deleting frees nothing, and the screen just refuses without saying why.

The obvious fix is to stop counting `deleted`, but the interesting part is
the question underneath it — whether a resource in `deleting` or `failed`
should hold quota — so it wants a decision, not a patch.

C6, small. Nexus, Tide and Flux each declare a Settings entry in their
module manifest and none of them has a page, so three sidebar links lead
to 404. Spark and Atlas have real ones and can serve as the mould if the
answer is to build rather than to remove the links.

separation is deliberate — identity and network are two grants — but the
screen never said so, so the user got a working username and password that
failed at first use with "no pg_hba.conf entry for host", an error that
names the host and never mentions Atlas. Unaudited issuance and silent
access requirements are one defect: the platform knew something important
about a credential and told nobody. On the live cluster that shape is
already there — one IPv4 /32 on a container reachable only over IPv6, a rule
present, plausible and incapable of ever matching.

The verdict is computed from the live rule table by a client-safe function
the service and the screen both call, so the trail and the UI cannot drift
into different stories: the event records whether the credential was
admitted when it was issued, and the credential UI renders an amber notice
naming what is actually missing — no rules at all, rules scoped to other
roles, or rules in the wrong address family — with a button to the tab that
fixes it. It says nothing when a rule already admits the user, because a
permanent banner is wallpaper by the second week and wrong on every cluster
whose firewall is correct.

The audit store's path is now overridable, for the same reason every other
store's is: tests that record audit events must not append to the
developer's real one.

title: fix(tide,spark,herald,atlas,courier): publish checks its result everywhere
body:
fix(tide,spark,herald,atlas,courier): publish checks its result everywhere

Flux and Nexus were taught to inspect the result of addPortForward before
marking a resource ready. The same defect was still live in Tide, Spark,
Herald and Courier, which fired the forward without awaiting it at all, and
in Atlas, which awaited it, read the result, and then console.errored and
marked the cluster active with its endpoint anyway. A log line on a server
nobody tails is not an operator-visible signal; from every seat that
matters it is indistinguishable from not checking.

All five now follow the shape set by the first pass. A failed publish makes
the resource degraded rather than active, the endpoint is not stored, and
the Herald event drops to partial carrying the port, the underlying error
and the address the resource would have had. Degraded rather than failed
because the container is up and the software installed — only a host NAT
rule is missing, every one of these failure paths rolls back by deleting
the container, and degraded is a live status for the port-forward
reconciler, so the rule comes back on the next pass and the resource
repairs in place. The endpoint is withheld because the detail pages render
their connection panels from the endpoint alone, without consulting status:
a stored endpoint is a published one as far as the customer is concerned.
Herald withholds lokiEndpoint on the same reasoning, and more urgently — a
log shipper pointed at a dead push URL drops silently, so the first sign of
trouble would be an empty log search hours later.

Courier is the case where degraded on its own says too little. It publishes
five well-known ports in a loop and they fail independently, and which one
is missing decides what happens next: 25 missing is an inbound outage
senders retry for days before bouncing, 587 missing is an outbound outage
the customer feels immediately, 993 missing means mail arrives and nobody
can read it, and 443 missing takes the Stalwart admin API with it. So each
missing port is named together with what stops working, the ports map
records only what actually published, and the event says plainly that no
reconciler covers Courier's forwards — they are fixed well-known numbers
rather than base+vmid and the reconciler walks only the seven products in
network/desired-state.ts, so promising an automatic repair would leave an
operator waiting for one that never comes.

Two consequences of recording a mail server as degraded had to be handled
alongside. ensureMailServer re-provisions a failed or deleting server from
scratch; degraded fell into that branch, which would have stood a second
container up beside a running Stalwart holding real mailboxes and leaked
the first one over a missing iptables rule, so a degraded server is now
returned as-is. And the two guards that gate mailbox and domain work on an
active server now accept degraded, because the admin API they use is
reached on the container's own address and no DNAT rule is involved —
refusing every remaining function of a working server because POP3 is
unreachable from the internet would be pure loss.

The verification test grows from Flux and Nexus to all seven. Stashing the
five provisioners and re-running turns the twelve new failure-path cases
red while all thirteen controls — every happy path, and the IPv6 pool where
there is no NAT to fail — stay green.

title: fix(data-products): pct exec has no /usr/local/bin, and it shows
body:
fix(data-products): pct exec has no /usr/local/bin, and it shows

The first Tide instance ever to provision came up healthy: mc and minio
in /usr/local/bin, the server listening on :9000, a bucket with two
objects in it. And every command the product runs inside it could not
find mc, because

    pct exec → PATH=/sbin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin

which is exactly where /usr/local/bin is not.

The consequence is a lie rather than an error. The metrics reader opens
with `command -v mc || exit 127`, so it exits, the response reports that
MinIO "did not answer `mc admin info`", and the operator goes looking at
a service that is running fine. The credential path has the same shape
and would have failed the same way — it predates this work, and no Tide
instance had ever existed to hit it.

Fixed at the seam rather than at the call site: `execInContainer` now
prepends the PATH, so every provisioner inherits it, and the metrics
reader (which goes through remote-exec directly) prepends the same
constant. Adding a directory takes none away, so nothing that works today
changes — rabbitmqctl in /usr/sbin and docker in /usr/bin are untouched.

Also documents, in the metrics file, that `admin info` counts come from
MinIO's background scanner: two objects uploaded read as zero for a
minute or two, then appeared. That is a lag in what MinIO knows, not a
gap in what we read, which is why it stays a number and not a null.

No test could have found this. It needed a container with software
installed in the place the platform installs software.

title: fix(atlas): revoke on the engine, reject in pg_hba, and delete what a failed provision made (#175)
body:
fix(atlas): revoke on the engine, reject in pg_hba, and delete what a failed provision made (#175)

Three things Atlas claimed and did not do.

Revoking a credential wrote a tombstone in the store and nothing else. The
row left the screen, the audit trail recorded that access had been withdrawn,
and the Postgres role kept its LOGIN attribute and every grant it was issued
with — so whoever held the password carried on connecting and reading data
indefinitely, with the platform reporting the opposite. Revocation now runs
ALTER ROLE ... NOLOGIN inside the primary container as the postgres
superuser, over the same path issuance uses. NOLOGIN rather than DROP ROLE
because DROP fails whenever the role owns an object or holds a grant, which
issuance guarantees by granting ALL PRIVILEGES on the database, and reassigning
ownership is a decision about someone's data that this endpoint cannot make.
A revocation that commonly fails is a revocation that commonly leaves the
access running.

NOLOGIN only stops the next connection, so the open sessions are terminated
too: the connections that matter here are pooled and live for days, and
without pg_terminate_backend "revoked" would mean "revoked whenever some
unrelated process happens to restart". The order is NOLOGIN first and the
kill second — reversed, the pooler reconnects within milliseconds and the
whole thing looks like it worked.

If either statement fails, the call returns DEPENDENCY_UNAVAILABLE and writes
nothing: no tombstone, no audit event. That is the rule credentialWiringFailed
already applies on the way in, and it exists because a store that claims a
withdrawal the engine never performed is worse than an error — nobody goes
looking for access they were told was already gone. The role name is derived
by one shared helper now, since issuance writes CREATE USER unquoted and
Postgres folds it to lower case; deriving it twice is how revocation would
start missing.

A deny firewall rule was generated as `hostnossl ... scram-sha-256`, which
denies nothing. hostnossl narrows a line to clients not using SSL and the
line still ends in an auth method, so the blocked host only had to skip TLS
to be let in with its password. Denies are now the pg_hba `reject` method,
emitted in the operator's own order — pg_hba is first-match, and nothing
reorders by action because "allow this host, reject its range" and "reject
this host, allow its range" are both legitimate and differ only by order.
Since a deny can now actually lock someone out, assessCredentialAccess models
the one arrangement it can prove — a /0 reject in the clients' address family
above every allow — and stays silent on everything narrower rather than tell
someone their working firewall is broken.

An HA provision kept its vmids in a local array written to the store only at
the last step, so a replica that failed mid-loop left the row saying
[primary] while replica containers ran on the node, and the failure path
released the IPs and deleted nothing. Containers are recorded the moment they
exist, and the rollback deletes them, releasing each address only once its
container is confirmed gone — an address handed back while an LXC still
answers on it is a duplicate IP on the shared L2. A container that survives
the rollback stays on the row with its address reserved and is named on the
Herald event, because the row is the only thing deprovisioning has to find it
by. The rollback is skipped once the cluster is recorded live, so a failing
Herald emit can no longer cost a customer their database.

title: fix(provisioning): one name for the default node
body:
fix(provisioning): one name for the default node

Flux provisioned against "pve", a node that does not exist on this
cluster, so every attempt died with `Proxmox request timed out` without
leaving `requested`. Three clusters in the block A smoke went that way.

The cause was not Flux. The setting had eleven readers in three shapes:

    PROXMOX_DEFAULT_NODE ?? "pve"                             (6 modules)
    DATA_PRODUCTS_DEFAULT_NODE ?? "pve"                       (2)
    DATA_PRODUCTS_DEFAULT_NODE ?? PROXMOX_DEFAULT_NODE ?? …   (3)

Production sets only PROXMOX_DEFAULT_NODE, so the second shape fell
through to the default. Flux had it — and so did `getDefaultNode()` in
provisioner-base, which means anything reaching for the shared helper
inherited the same wrong answer.

Fixing Flux alone would have left nine copies and the same trap for the
next module, so the eleven readers become one: data-products/default-node
accepts either spelling, keeps "pve" as the last resort because it is
Proxmox's own default for a single-node install, and every store and the
provisioner base re-export it.

The test pins the case that broke: PROXMOX_DEFAULT_NODE set on its own
resolves to that node, which is exactly how production is configured and
exactly what Flux could not do.

title: fix(core): encrypt stopped working above 64 KB, and nothing said so
body:
fix(core): encrypt stopped working above 64 KB, and nothing said so

`encrypt()` ended in `btoa(String.fromCharCode(...result))`. That spread
puts one call argument on the stack per ciphertext byte, and V8 refuses
past roughly 64-128 KB with `RangeError: Maximum call stack size
exceeded` — measured on the Node 22 that runs our suites, the boundary
falls between 65536 and 131072 bytes.

The damage is in the asymmetry. `decrypt()` never spread anything, so a
store that grew past the ceiling kept LOADING perfectly while every save
threw. The file on disk froze at its last small version, the UI kept
rendering the stale-but-plausible contents it had just read, and the
only trace was a log line per lost record. The dev
`.herald-events-store.json` was hitting this on every test round,
reporting "FAILED to persist ... this event is lost". Production runs
STORE_BACKEND=postgres and so escapes it today, but the code default is
`json` — any deployment left on the default is one large store away from
the same silent freeze.

The fix builds the binary string in 32 KiB chunks instead of one spread.
Compatibility is not an argument about intent, it is structural: the
chunking happens on the binary string, not on the base64, and `btoa` is
still called exactly once over the assembled whole. For every input the
old code could handle, the new encoder emits the identical string —
asserted directly, not inferred, across the padding-sensitive lengths
and both sides of the chunk seam. Every `.{module}-store.json` and
`.connections.json` written by an older build keeps decrypting, and a
store written by this build stays readable by an older build, which is
what makes a rollback safe.

`btoa`/`atob` rather than Node's `Buffer` on purpose: this module is
consumed from browser and edge bundles as well as Node, and those two
globals plus `crypto` are the only ones the file has ever assumed.

The base64 -> bytes direction was never the stack bug (`Uint8Array.from`
takes an iterable, not an argument list), but it walked the string by
code point through the iterator protocol and was only correct because
atob output stays inside U+0000..U+00FF; it now reads by code unit.

`scripts/migrate-stores/state/crypto.ts` is a deliberate standalone copy
of this module and carried the same defect — on a script whose entire
job is reading the large store files. Fixed identically.

packages/core had no test runner; it gets vitest and a `tests/` dir
outside the tsc `include`, so tests never reach dist. The suite pins the
defect with a 1 MB round-trip: with the spread restored, that case and
the 128 KB one fail with the exact RangeError, and the other thirteen
still pass — which is precisely how a small-payloads-only suite let this
ship.

docs: deleting a resource does not give the quota back (#156)

Two findings from the 2026-08-19 smoke, both registered rather than

deleting frees nothing, and the screen just refuses without saying why.

should hold quota — so it wants a decision, not a patch.

module manifest and none of them has a page, so three sidebar links lead

title: fix(provisioners): allocate the vmid with the container everywhere (#166)
body:
fix(provisioners): allocate the vmid with the container everywhere (#166)

/cluster/nextid answers with the lowest free id and does not reserve it, so
two provisions starting in the same second read the same number, the first
POST wins, and the second dies with "CT 104 already exists" and stays failed
forever over an id that was taken for a few milliseconds. The fix already
existed as createLxcWithFreshVmid in data-products/provisioner-base, adopted
in tide, flux and nexus; every other provisioner still called getNextVmid()
and createLxcContainer() as two separate steps with that window between them.

Adopted at all ten remaining sites: atlas primary and replica, beacon's
postgres and PowerDNS containers plus the orchestrator's scale-up, email,
herald, launch, spark, and both mesh runtime-adapter sites (provision and
scale). A grep for getNextVmid now finds it only in provisioner-base itself
and in the helper's own test. Ignite and blaze are untouched by request —
another change owns those files.

Where the container's address is a function of the id, the config is built
inside the per-attempt callback so a retry re-derives it: beacon and herald
both call allocateLxcIp(node, vmid), and a config built once against the
losing id would have put that id's address on the winning container. On this
cluster vmbr1 is a single L2 spanning both nodes, so a duplicate address is a
black hole rather than an error. Where the address comes from a Mesh
reservation instead — atlas, email, launch, spark — the reservation stays
outside the callback so a retry reuses it rather than leaking a second one.

Two call sites needed more than a mechanical rewrite. Atlas's replica loop
was the one worth thinking about: a mid-loop retry has to be safe against the
function's rollback, and it is, because the rollback is
releaseClusterAllocations(), which matches allocations by serviceId and knows
nothing about vmids, and because the retry happens before anything about that
replica is persisted. Its Mesh reservation is now made before the create
rather than after the id, so a retry does not burn a second address. Launch
wrote its replica row before creating the container; that row carries the
vmid, and both rollbackReplica and deprovisionReplica stop and delete by that
field, so a losing id persisted there would have torn down whichever
container won the race. The row is now written after the create, against the
id that took.

The helper's own retry behaviour is already covered next door in
vmid-collision.test.ts and is not duplicated. What is pinned here instead is
the thing that test cannot see: provisioner-vmid-adoption.test.ts drives
Herald's real provisioner with the real helper and only Proxmox faked
underneath, and asserts that the losing attempt's config carried .104, the
winning one carried .105, and that lxcIds and the PORT_BASE + vmid forward
both came out as 105. Herald was chosen because its address and its published
port are both vmid-derived, so a config built once would show up in the
assertions rather than hiding. tests/mesh/09 replaced provisioner-base
wholesale with a strict mock naming getNextVmid and createLxcContainer; it
now delegates to the real helper through the deps seam instead.

title: fix(ignite): verify the publish, and stop the invoke test racing itself (#174)
body:
fix(ignite): verify the publish, and stop the invoke test racing itself (#174)

Ignite was the last provisioner calling `addPortForward` fire-and-forget. It
then marked the function `active`, stored its endpoint URL and emitted a
`success` event, with nothing having checked whether the host DNAT rule was
ever installed. `addPortForward` resolves `{ok:false}` instead of throwing —
that is how it reports a lost race for /run/xtables.lock against Docker — so
the catch block never saw it. The result was a green function handing out a
URL that refused every request: the tenant wires that URL into a webhook or a
cron and finds out hours later, from something missing downstream, that it
never worked. The forward is now awaited and its result read, the endpoint is
not stored when it did not publish, and the Herald event drops to `partial`
naming the port, the underlying error and the address the function would have
had.

Recording that outcome needed a status Ignite did not have, so this adds
`degraded` to FunctionStatus rather than reusing an existing member, and says
so plainly because it is a platform type change plus migration 0037. The
alternatives are all worse. `active` is the defect. `failed` is wrong twice
over: the provision did not die — the container is up and the runtime is
installed and serving on 8080 — and nothing transitions out of `failed`, so
the function would sit red forever holding the org's tier slot while its LXC
stayed on the node, and an operator reading "failed" reasonably rebuilds,
leaking the container that is still running. `deploying` would claim work is
in flight when nothing is running. `degraded` is what every other data
product already uses for exactly this state, and — the part that makes it
repair rather than merely honest — it is a live status for the port-forward
reconciler, which already carries an `ignite` descriptor on base 7000 → 8080
and collects Ignite functions. A function left degraded is picked up on the
next pass and its missing rule re-applied. The migration only ADDs the enum
value; no existing row is rewritten, because nothing here can tell a working
forward from a missing one. The badge renders it amber rather than red for
the same reason the reconciler matters, and the service's deletable states
gain it so a degraded function is not the one thing a tenant cannot remove.

The second half is a genuinely flaky test. tests/ignite/03-api-routes
registered `vi.mock` for the provisioner twice, and vi.mock on one path is
last-one-wins, so the second block silently replaced the first. The first
existed to keep background writes out of the store: every store write is a
read-modify-write of a single JSON file, so a write that began before a later
test created its function rewrites the file without it and that test answers
404. It achieved this by making `invokeFunction` never settle, which also
meant the invoke path was never exercised past "queued". The override made it
resolve and put the race straight back — the file failed 3 of 6 baseline
runs, always on `data.id starts with 'iginv-'`. There is now one mock that
resolves, and the three tests that trigger the fire-and-forget chain wait for
its tail — the function's invocationCount bump — before returning, which is a
real happens-after signal rather than a sleep. Ten consecutive runs pass.

One test mock had to move with the code: 08-terminal-status stubbed
`addPortForward` as resolving `undefined`, which was harmless while nobody
read the result and became a thrown TypeError once somebody did. It now
returns the real `{ok:true}` shape.
