title: fix(ignite,blaze): a successful delete is deleted, not failed
body:
fix(ignite,blaze): a successful delete is deleted, not failed

Ignite and Blaze had no terminal status. FunctionStatus and WorkerStatus
both stopped at `deleting`, so when deprovisioning finished — every
container stopped, every container removed — the provisioner had nowhere
to put that outcome and wrote `failed` instead. The teardown had gone
perfectly and the record said it had broken.

That single write cost two things at once. On screen, a function or
worker the tenant deleted on purpose carried the same status and the same
red badge as one whose provisioning had died; nobody, support included,
could tell the two apart afterwards. And because nothing ever transitions
out of `failed`, and `failed` correctly consumes quota — the LXC a broken
provision created is usually still sitting on the node — every deliberate
delete burned a tier slot permanently. On starter, which allows two, two
deletes locked an org out of the product with no action available to them
that would ever free it again. This is the same lockout #163 fixed for
Nexus, Atlas, Spark and Tide, except the fix there keys on a terminal
`deleted` status that these two products did not have.

So `deleted` is added to both unions, to both Postgres status enums via
migration 0036, and to both status badges, where it renders as a muted
tombstone rather than falling through to a default. The provisioners now
decide between the two outcomes on evidence: they track which containers
could not be removed, and land on `deleted` only when nothing was left
behind, keeping `failed` — and the failure event in Herald — for the case
where an LXC is still on the node and the capacity genuinely has not come
back. A failed stop no longer counts against that, since Proxmox deletes
running containers and an already-stopped one cannot be stopped again.

With a terminal status to key on, both tier checks adopt the shared
countTowardQuota helper, which releases a slot for `deleted` alone and
keeps counting `failed` and `deleting`. That asymmetry is the point of
the helper and is now pinned from both sides: a deprovisioned resource
must not be `failed`, a genuinely failed provision must still be, and
create → delete → create must no longer exhaust a starter tier. Ignite's
store also stops re-declaring FunctionStatus and re-exports the platform
type, which is how it drifted a member behind in the first place.

The `"deleted"` type error that tests/ignite/04 has been carrying in the
accepted baseline for weeks disappears with this change: that test was
reaching for the status that should have existed all along.

title: fix(flux,nexus): publish checks its result before marking active (#167)
body:
fix(flux,nexus): publish checks its result before marking active (#167)

`addPortForward` was made awaitable and result-returning on 2026-08-15
precisely so a failed port-forward would stop being invisible. Flux and
Nexus never got updated and kept calling it fire-and-forget, so the
provisioner marked the cluster `active`, stored an endpoint and emitted a
`success` event without ever knowing whether the host would forward
anything to the container.

What that costs a user is the worst shape a failure can take: not an
error, but a lie. They are told the cluster is ready, handed an address,
and the address refuses connections. Nothing in the UI, the event feed or
the status disagrees with the claim, so the time goes into doubting their
own client, their firewall and their credentials before anyone thinks to
check a NAT rule on the host. The failure is not hypothetical here — the
publish has lost the race for /run/xtables.lock against Docker, which is
why the iptables calls carry `-w 5` — and `addPortForward` resolves
`{ok:false}` rather than throwing, so nothing above it fails loudly on its
own. Inspecting the result is the only thing between a lost lock and a
customer holding a dead address.

Both call sites now await it and act on the outcome. A port that was not
published is not recorded on the cluster: the detail page renders its
connection panel from `endpoint` alone, without consulting status, so a
stored endpoint is a published one as far as the user is concerned. The
cluster goes `degraded` rather than `failed`, because the container is up
and the broker or engine is installed and running — only a host NAT rule
is missing. Tearing down working state over a contended lock would be a
worse outcome than an amber badge, and `degraded` is a live status for the

body:
fix(tide,spark,herald,atlas,courier): publish checks its result everywhere

Flux and Nexus were taught to inspect the result of addPortForward before
marking a resource ready. The same defect was still live in Tide, Spark,
Herald and Courier, which fired the forward without awaiting it at all, and
in Atlas, which awaited it, read the result, and then console.errored and
marked the cluster active with its endpoint anyway. A log line on a server
nobody tails is not an operator-visible signal; from every seat that
matters it is indistinguishable from not checking.

All five now follow the shape set by the first pass. A failed publish makes
the resource degraded rather than active, the endpoint is not stored, and
the Herald event drops to partial carrying the port, the underlying error
and the address the resource would have had. Degraded rather than failed
because the container is up and the software installed — only a host NAT
rule is missing, every one of these failure paths rolls back by deleting
the container, and degraded is a live status for the port-forward
reconciler, so the rule comes back on the next pass and the resource
repairs in place. The endpoint is withheld because the detail pages render
their connection panels from the endpoint alone, without consulting status:
a stored endpoint is a published one as far as the customer is concerned.
Herald withholds lokiEndpoint on the same reasoning, and more urgently — a
log shipper pointed at a dead push URL drops silently, so the first sign of
trouble would be an empty log search hours later.

Courier is the case where degraded on its own says too little. It publishes
five well-known ports in a loop and they fail independently, and which one
is missing decides what happens next: 25 missing is an inbound outage
senders retry for days before bouncing, 587 missing is an outbound outage
the customer feels immediately, 993 missing means mail arrives and nobody
can read it, and 443 missing takes the Stalwart admin API with it. So each
missing port is named together with what stops working, the ports map
records only what actually published, and the event says plainly that no
reconciler covers Courier's forwards — they are fixed well-known numbers
rather than base+vmid and the reconciler walks only the seven products in
network/desired-state.ts, so promising an automatic repair would leave an
operator waiting for one that never comes.

Two consequences of recording a mail server as degraded had to be handled
alongside. ensureMailServer re-provisions a failed or deleting server from
scratch; degraded fell into that branch, which would have stood a second
container up beside a running Stalwart holding real mailboxes and leaked
the first one over a missing iptables rule, so a degraded server is now
returned as-is. And the two guards that gate mailbox and domain work on an
active server now accept degraded, because the admin API they use is
reached on the container's own address and no DNAT rule is involved —
refusing every remaining function of a working server because POP3 is
unreachable from the internet would be pure loss.

The verification test grows from Flux and Nexus to all seven. Stashing the
five provisioners and re-running turns the twelve new failure-path cases
red while all thirteen controls — every happy path, and the IPv6 pool where
there is no NAT to fail — stay green.

title: fix(web): stop seeding form state from effects
body:
fix(web): stop seeding form state from effects

Thirty-six `react-hooks/set-state-in-effect` errors across thirty-five files
were one mistake repeated: a dialog or page would declare its fields with empty
`useState` defaults, then run an effect whose only job was to overwrite them
with the props or query data the component already had. The effect was doing
work React does for free.

The cost is a wasted render, and it is not invisible. React renders once with
the empty defaults, commits that to the DOM, runs the effect, and renders again
with the real values. Every edit dialog in this app therefore painted blank
inputs before showing the record you clicked on. Where the seeding effect
listed a query result in its dependencies, the cascade was worse than cosmetic:
the query client refetches on a thirty second interval, so a background refetch
re-ran the effect and silently discarded whatever the operator had typed into
an unsaved firewall rule or SDN zone.

Three techniques replace it, chosen per case rather than applied uniformly.
Most dialogs now split into a shell that owns the chrome and a form component
rendered inside `DialogContent`; Radix unmounts that subtree on close, so React
re-runs the `useState` initialisers on the next open and the reset branch of
the old effect disappears. A `key` on the form covers the remaining job, which
is re-seeding when the dialog is repointed at a different record while still
open. Values that were only ever derived from other state, such as the Mesh
child-prefix clamp and the default domain in the email pages, are now computed
during render and stored nowhere. Genuinely external state reads its own source
directly through `useSyncExternalStore`: the viewport query in `SplitView` and
the localStorage-backed onboarding checklist, which was keeping a copy of
localStorage in React state and filling the copy from an effect.

Two effects turned out to be dead. Both member-dialog tabs render inside
`DialogContent` and cleared themselves when `open` went false, which could only
ever happen during the closing animation, blanking the form as it faded out.

Behaviour is preserved deliberately, including behaviour that is arguably
wrong. The migrate dialog's defaults were chosen once per open and never
revised, an intent its `eslint-disable-line` made explicit, so its form is
mounted without a key to keep exactly that. Atlas consumes its one-shot
`?create=true` on close now rather than on open, because stripping the param
while the dialog was up would flip the key underneath it.

title: fix(nexus): stop blaming a restart that never happened (#155)
body:
fix(nexus): stop blaming a restart that never happened (#155)

The first ScyllaDB cluster to reach `active` in production answered:

    "cpuPercent": 3, "memoryPercent": 66, "diskPercent": 11,
    "nodeState": "UN", "nodeHealthy": true,
    "readOpsPerSec": null, "writeOpsPerSec": null,
    "unavailable": ["Operation rates: the two samples of ScyllaDB's
     counters could not be compared, which happens when the node
     restarted between them."]

The container and the ring were measured correctly — that is the parser
working against real nodetool output. The explanation was false. Nothing
restarted: a brand-new cluster simply has no keyspace of its own yet, and
there was already a branch saying exactly that, which could never run.

`keyspaces` used null to mean "tablestats did not answer" and an empty
array to mean "no user keyspaces", but the reading collapsed both into
null, so the honest branch was skipped and the wrong one spoke. Those are
different facts and they now travel separately: `tablestatsRead` says
whether the command produced anything, `keyspaces` is the filtered list.
ScyllaDB always has internal keyspaces, so any keyspace block at all is
proof the command ran.

A wrong explanation is worse than a vague one — it sends an operator
looking for a restart that never happened. That is the same defect this
module was written to remove, one level up: not an invented number, an
invented reason.

Found by provisioning a real cluster. The suites only ever see an
unreachable node, where the branch is never reached.

title: fix(data-products): /cluster/nextid does not reserve, so stop trusting it (#161)
body:
fix(data-products): /cluster/nextid does not reserve, so stop trusting it (#161)

Two resources created in the same second got the same vmid and the second
one died permanently:

    Failed to create LXC on sp1-sd-catalisatec-2: 500
    {"message":"CT 104 already exists on node 'sp1-sd-catalisatec-2'"}

getNextVmid() is a bare GET of Proxmox /cluster/nextid. That endpoint
answers with the lowest free id and does not reserve it, so concurrent
provisions all read the same number. The first POST won; the rest got the
500 above, it propagated out of the provisioner, and the resource was
marked failed with no retry on a fresh id. Seen live: three Flux clusters
created in the same second, all handed 104, one survived. Anyone clicking
create three times, or provisioning in batch, hit this.

The gap between reading an id and using it cannot be closed on the read
side — Proxmox has no reserving allocator to call. So it is closed on the
write side instead: createLxcWithFreshVmid makes allocation and creation
one retryable unit. It reads an id, tries to create, and on that specific
conflict throws the id away and reads a fresh one, up to five times. By
the time it asks again Proxmox has recorded the container that won, so the
next id is genuinely free.

Two details are deliberate. The retry fires only for a recognisable "that
id is taken" — anything else propagates untouched on the first attempt,
because retrying a real error would turn one legible failure into five,
hammer whatever is already broken, and bury the cause. And the config is
rebuilt per attempt, because Flux and Nexus derive the container's IP from
the vmid and Tide derives its egress NIC from it; a config built once
against the losing id would carry that id's address onto the winning
container, which on this cluster is the duplicate-IP failure mode that
takes hours to find.

The helper returns the vmid that actually took. Callers persist it as
lxcIds and roll back with it, so returning the first id read would leave
the platform stopping, exec'ing into, and eventually deleting somebody
else's container.

Adopted in the three provisioners the production smoke exercises — Tide,
Flux and Nexus. The other callers of getNextVmid (atlas, beacon, blaze,
email, herald, ignite, launch, spark, and the mesh runtime-adapter) are
left alone on purpose: they have the same defect, but nothing here can
exercise them, and refactoring what cannot be tested is how a race gets
traded for a regression. They are a follow-up.

Tests pin both halves of the contract: a create that collides once
succeeds on the next id, and a create that fails for any other reason is
attempted exactly once.

title: fix(core): encrypt stopped working above 64 KB, and nothing said so (#160)
body:
fix(core): encrypt stopped working above 64 KB, and nothing said so (#160)

`encrypt()` ended in `btoa(String.fromCharCode(...result))`. That spread
puts one call argument on the stack per ciphertext byte, and V8 refuses
past roughly 64-128 KB with `RangeError: Maximum call stack size
exceeded` — measured on the Node 22 that runs our suites, the boundary
falls between 65536 and 131072 bytes.

The damage is in the asymmetry. `decrypt()` never spread anything, so a
store that grew past the ceiling kept LOADING perfectly while every save
threw. The file on disk froze at its last small version, the UI kept
rendering the stale-but-plausible contents it had just read, and the
only trace was a log line per lost record. The dev
`.herald-events-store.json` was hitting this on every test round,
reporting "FAILED to persist ... this event is lost". Production runs
STORE_BACKEND=postgres and so escapes it today, but the code default is
`json` — any deployment left on the default is one large store away from
the same silent freeze.

The fix builds the binary string in 32 KiB chunks instead of one spread.
Compatibility is not an argument about intent, it is structural: the
chunking happens on the binary string, not on the base64, and `btoa` is
still called exactly once over the assembled whole. For every input the
old code could handle, the new encoder emits the identical string —
asserted directly, not inferred, across the padding-sensitive lengths
and both sides of the chunk seam. Every `.{module}-store.json` and
`.connections.json` written by an older build keeps decrypting, and a
store written by this build stays readable by an older build, which is
what makes a rollback safe.

`btoa`/`atob` rather than Node's `Buffer` on purpose: this module is
consumed from browser and edge bundles as well as Node, and those two
globals plus `crypto` are the only ones the file has ever assumed.

The base64 -> bytes direction was never the stack bug (`Uint8Array.from`
takes an iterable, not an argument list), but it walked the string by
code point through the iterator protocol and was only correct because
atob output stays inside U+0000..U+00FF; it now reads by code unit.

`scripts/migrate-stores/state/crypto.ts` is a deliberate standalone copy
of this module and carried the same defect — on a script whose entire
job is reading the large store files. Fixed identically.

packages/core had no test runner; it gets vitest and a `tests/` dir
outside the tsc `include`, so tests never reach dist. The suite pins the
defect with a 1 MB round-trip: with the spread restored, that case and
the 128 KB one fail with the exact RangeError, and the other thirteen
still pass — which is precisely how a small-payloads-only suite let this
ship.

title: fix(mesh): call every hook before the redirect bail-out (#162)
body:
fix(mesh): call every hook before the redirect bail-out (#162)

A hook that only runs on some renders is not a lint nit, it is a tab that
dies. React matches hooks by call order, so the render where the order
changes throws, the error boundary catches it, and the user gets
"Something went wrong" where a page used to be — no data, no retry, no
hint at what happened. That is how the Herald tab fell over.

The Mesh services page had exactly that shape. It returned null early to
let the ?create= redirect take over, and only afterwards called useMemo
twice for the filtered list and the summary counters. Any visit carrying
that query param rendered with two fewer hooks than the visit before it.

The two useMemo calls now sit above the bail-out, and the early return
moved down to just after the last hook. `services` picked up a useMemo of
its own so the two downstream memos stop seeing a fresh array identity on
every render. Nothing the page renders changed.

Also renamed the module-private `usePostgres()` predicate to
`isPostgresBacked()` in the deploy and sshkeys stores. That is server
code with no React in it, but the `use` prefix made the hooks lint rule
treat every call as a misplaced hook and bury the real error above in
noise. Behaviour is untouched — same env lookup, same boolean.

The remaining rules-of-hooks errors are all in tests/, where the helper
is named `useTestSession`. Same false positive from the naming
convention, left alone deliberately.

    DATA_PRODUCTS_DEFAULT_NODE ?? "pve"                       (2)

provisioner base re-export it.

title: fix(data-products): stop counting deleted resources against tier limits (#163)
body:
fix(data-products): stop counting deleted resources against tier limits (#163)

Deletes in the data products are soft: the row survives with status
"deleted" so the audit trail and the historical view keep their record.
Nexus, Atlas, Spark and Tide each computed the tier check by listing on
orgId alone and handing the raw length to checkTierLimit, so those
tombstones counted as live capacity. On production a starter org that
created two clusters and deleted both was permanently at its limit —
TIER_LIMIT_EXCEEDED with details.current of 2, both of them deleted —
and unrecoverable from the product, because nothing transitions out of
"deleted".

The count now goes through a shared countTowardQuota helper in
data-products/quota.ts rather than four copies of the same filter, on
the same reasoning that moved DNS and default-node resolution into their
own leaf modules: this codebase keeps paying for logic that lives in N
places and gets fixed in one.

"deleted" is the only status that releases a slot, and that asymmetry is
the point. A failed provision has usually already created its container
and only deprovisioning removes it, so releasing at "failed" lets a
tenant loop create-fail-create and accumulate real containers past the
capacity they pay for. A resource in "deleting" still has its container
up right now, so freeing the slot before teardown finishes lets the
replacement come up alongside it. Only the terminal status proves the
capacity actually came back.

title: fix(provisioners): allocate the vmid with the container everywhere
body:
fix(provisioners): allocate the vmid with the container everywhere

/cluster/nextid answers with the lowest free id and does not reserve it, so
two provisions starting in the same second read the same number, the first
POST wins, and the second dies with "CT 104 already exists" and stays failed
forever over an id that was taken for a few milliseconds. The fix already
existed as createLxcWithFreshVmid in data-products/provisioner-base, adopted
in tide, flux and nexus; every other provisioner still called getNextVmid()
and createLxcContainer() as two separate steps with that window between them.

Adopted at all ten remaining sites: atlas primary and replica, beacon's
postgres and PowerDNS containers plus the orchestrator's scale-up, email,
herald, launch, spark, and both mesh runtime-adapter sites (provision and
scale). A grep for getNextVmid now finds it only in provisioner-base itself
and in the helper's own test. Ignite and blaze are untouched by request —
another change owns those files.

Where the container's address is a function of the id, the config is built
inside the per-attempt callback so a retry re-derives it: beacon and herald
both call allocateLxcIp(node, vmid), and a config built once against the
losing id would have put that id's address on the winning container. On this
cluster vmbr1 is a single L2 spanning both nodes, so a duplicate address is a
black hole rather than an error. Where the address comes from a Mesh
reservation instead — atlas, email, launch, spark — the reservation stays
outside the callback so a retry reuses it rather than leaking a second one.

Two call sites needed more than a mechanical rewrite. Atlas's replica loop
was the one worth thinking about: a mid-loop retry has to be safe against the
function's rollback, and it is, because the rollback is
releaseClusterAllocations(), which matches allocations by serviceId and knows
nothing about vmids, and because the retry happens before anything about that
replica is persisted. Its Mesh reservation is now made before the create
rather than after the id, so a retry does not burn a second address. Launch
wrote its replica row before creating the container; that row carries the
vmid, and both rollbackReplica and deprovisionReplica stop and delete by that
field, so a losing id persisted there would have torn down whichever
container won the race. The row is now written after the create, against the
id that took.

The helper's own retry behaviour is already covered next door in
vmid-collision.test.ts and is not duplicated. What is pinned here instead is
the thing that test cannot see: provisioner-vmid-adoption.test.ts drives
Herald's real provisioner with the real helper and only Proxmox faked
underneath, and asserts that the losing attempt's config carried .104, the
winning one carried .105, and that lxcIds and the PORT_BASE + vmid forward
both came out as 105. Herald was chosen because its address and its published
port are both vmid-derived, so a config built once would show up in the
assertions rather than hiding. tests/mesh/09 replaced provisioner-base
wholesale with a strict mock naming getNextVmid and createLxcContainer; it
now delegates to the real helper through the deps seam instead.

title: fix(ignite,blaze): a successful delete is deleted, not failed (#169)
body:
fix(ignite,blaze): a successful delete is deleted, not failed (#169)

Ignite and Blaze had no terminal status. FunctionStatus and WorkerStatus
both stopped at `deleting`, so when deprovisioning finished — every
container stopped, every container removed — the provisioner had nowhere
to put that outcome and wrote `failed` instead. The teardown had gone
perfectly and the record said it had broken.

That single write cost two things at once. On screen, a function or
worker the tenant deleted on purpose carried the same status and the same
red badge as one whose provisioning had died; nobody, support included,
could tell the two apart afterwards. And because nothing ever transitions
out of `failed`, and `failed` correctly consumes quota — the LXC a broken
provision created is usually still sitting on the node — every deliberate
delete burned a tier slot permanently. On starter, which allows two, two
deletes locked an org out of the product with no action available to them
that would ever free it again. This is the same lockout #163 fixed for
Nexus, Atlas, Spark and Tide, except the fix there keys on a terminal
`deleted` status that these two products did not have.

So `deleted` is added to both unions, to both Postgres status enums via
migration 0036, and to both status badges, where it renders as a muted
tombstone rather than falling through to a default. The provisioners now
decide between the two outcomes on evidence: they track which containers
could not be removed, and land on `deleted` only when nothing was left
behind, keeping `failed` — and the failure event in Herald — for the case
where an LXC is still on the node and the capacity genuinely has not come
back. A failed stop no longer counts against that, since Proxmox deletes
running containers and an already-stopped one cannot be stopped again.

With a terminal status to key on, both tier checks adopt the shared
countTowardQuota helper, which releases a slot for `deleted` alone and
keeps counting `failed` and `deleting`. That asymmetry is the point of
the helper and is now pinned from both sides: a deprovisioned resource
must not be `failed`, a genuinely failed provision must still be, and
create → delete → create must no longer exhaust a starter tier. Ignite's
store also stops re-declaring FunctionStatus and re-exports the platform
type, which is how it drifted a member behind in the first place.

The `"deleted"` type error that tests/ignite/04 has been carrying in the
accepted baseline for weeks disappears with this change: that test was
reaching for the status that should have existed all along.

title: fix(data-products): stop counting deleted resources against tier limits
body:
fix(data-products): stop counting deleted resources against tier limits

Deletes in the data products are soft: the row survives with status
"deleted" so the audit trail and the historical view keep their record.
Nexus, Atlas, Spark and Tide each computed the tier check by listing on
orgId alone and handing the raw length to checkTierLimit, so those
tombstones counted as live capacity. On production a starter org that
created two clusters and deleted both was permanently at its limit —
TIER_LIMIT_EXCEEDED with details.current of 2, both of them deleted —
and unrecoverable from the product, because nothing transitions out of
"deleted".

The count now goes through a shared countTowardQuota helper in
data-products/quota.ts rather than four copies of the same filter, on
the same reasoning that moved DNS and default-node resolution into their
own leaf modules: this codebase keeps paying for logic that lives in N
places and gets fixed in one.

"deleted" is the only status that releases a slot, and that asymmetry is
the point. A failed provision has usually already created its container
and only deprovisioning removes it, so releasing at "failed" lets a
tenant loop create-fail-create and accumulate real containers past the
capacity they pay for. A resource in "deleting" still has its container
up right now, so freeing the slot before teardown finishes lets the
replacement come up alongside it. Only the terminal status proves the
capacity actually came back.

title: fix(nexus): stop blaming a restart that never happened
body:
fix(nexus): stop blaming a restart that never happened

The first ScyllaDB cluster to reach `active` in production answered:

    "cpuPercent": 3, "memoryPercent": 66, "diskPercent": 11,
    "nodeState": "UN", "nodeHealthy": true,
    "readOpsPerSec": null, "writeOpsPerSec": null,
    "unavailable": ["Operation rates: the two samples of ScyllaDB's
     counters could not be compared, which happens when the node
     restarted between them."]

The container and the ring were measured correctly — that is the parser
working against real nodetool output. The explanation was false. Nothing
restarted: a brand-new cluster simply has no keyspace of its own yet, and
there was already a branch saying exactly that, which could never run.

`keyspaces` used null to mean "tablestats did not answer" and an empty
array to mean "no user keyspaces", but the reading collapsed both into
null, so the honest branch was skipped and the wrong one spoke. Those are
different facts and they now travel separately: `tablestatsRead` says
whether the command produced anything, `keyspaces` is the filtered list.
ScyllaDB always has internal keyspaces, so any keyspace block at all is
proof the command ran.

A wrong explanation is worse than a vague one — it sends an operator
looking for a restart that never happened. That is the same defect this
module was written to remove, one level up: not an invented number, an
invented reason.

Found by provisioning a real cluster. The suites only ever see an
unreachable node, where the branch is never reached.

title: fix(mesh): call every hook before the redirect bail-out
body:
fix(mesh): call every hook before the redirect bail-out

A hook that only runs on some renders is not a lint nit, it is a tab that
dies. React matches hooks by call order, so the render where the order
changes throws, the error boundary catches it, and the user gets
"Something went wrong" where a page used to be — no data, no retry, no
hint at what happened. That is how the Herald tab fell over.

The Mesh services page had exactly that shape. It returned null early to
let the ?create= redirect take over, and only afterwards called useMemo
twice for the filtered list and the summary counters. Any visit carrying
that query param rendered with two fewer hooks than the visit before it.

The two useMemo calls now sit above the bail-out, and the early return
moved down to just after the last hook. `services` picked up a useMemo of
its own so the two downstream memos stop seeing a fresh array identity on
every render. Nothing the page renders changed.

Also renamed the module-private `usePostgres()` predicate to
`isPostgresBacked()` in the deploy and sshkeys stores. That is server
code with no React in it, but the `use` prefix made the hooks lint rule
treat every call as a misplaced hook and bury the real error above in
noise. Behaviour is untouched — same env lookup, same boolean.

The remaining rules-of-hooks errors are all in tests/, where the helper
is named `useTestSession`. Same false positive from the naming
convention, left alone deliberately.

title: fix(data-products): pct exec has no /usr/local/bin, and it shows (#158)
body:
fix(data-products): pct exec has no /usr/local/bin, and it shows (#158)

The first Tide instance ever to provision came up healthy: mc and minio
in /usr/local/bin, the server listening on :9000, a bucket with two
objects in it. And every command the product runs inside it could not
find mc, because

    pct exec → PATH=/sbin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin

which is exactly where /usr/local/bin is not.

The consequence is a lie rather than an error. The metrics reader opens
with `command -v mc || exit 127`, so it exits, the response reports that
MinIO "did not answer `mc admin info`", and the operator goes looking at
a service that is running fine. The credential path has the same shape
and would have failed the same way — it predates this work, and no Tide
instance had ever existed to hit it.

Fixed at the seam rather than at the call site: `execInContainer` now
prepends the PATH, so every provisioner inherits it, and the metrics
reader (which goes through remote-exec directly) prepends the same
constant. Adding a directory takes none away, so nothing that works today
changes — rabbitmqctl in /usr/sbin and docker in /usr/bin are untouched.

Also documents, in the metrics file, that `admin info` counts come from
MinIO's background scanner: two objects uploaded read as zero for a
minute or two, then appeared. That is a lag in what MinIO knows, not a
gap in what we read, which is why it stays a number and not a null.

No test could have found this. It needed a container with software
installed in the place the platform installs software.

title: feat(tide): a way out for a container that only has IPv6
body:
feat(tide): a way out for a container that only has IPv6

Every Mesh pool here is IPv6-only, which is why a Tide container needs no
DNAT to be reached. It is also why it cannot reach `dl.min.io`, which has
no AAAA record, so MinIO could never be downloaded and no Tide instance
ever finished provisioning. The download failed in two milliseconds with
"Could not connect to server" — network-unreachable wearing a connection
error's clothes.

The container now keeps its public IPv6 on eth0 for inbound and gains a
private IPv4 on eth1 purely to get out. That costs no public address:
172.10.0.0/24 is RFC1918 and the host has masqueraded it out of its single
public IPv4 since this cluster existed —

    -A POSTROUTING -s 172.10.0.0/24 -o vmbr0 -j MASQUERADE

which is how every other guest installs packages. Two default routes, one
per address family, which do not compete.

`firewall=0` on the new NIC is not decoration. With firewall=1 Proxmox
builds an fwbr bridge in front of it and NAT egress breaks inside an
unprivileged LXC, with apt failing "Could not resolve host" — the exact
symptom this interface exists to remove. eth0 pins it for the same reason
and the test pins it here.

The address comes from `allocateLxcIp`, which scans every guest's every
NIC and throws rather than fall back to a scheme that cannot see what is
taken. That matters more than usual: vmbr1 is one L2 spanning both nodes,
so a duplicate is not a clash, it is a black hole for whoever loses the
ARP race.

Tide only. Spark installs over apt and Email uses a host with IPv6; both
work today and touching them would be risk without a defect. The helper is
shared so the next module that hits this wall inherits it.

NAT64/DNS64 at the gateway remains the larger, better answer — it fixes
this for every IPv6-only guest at once and needs no second NIC. It also
cannot help anything dialling a literal IPv4 address, since nothing asks
DNS then. This is the smaller, reversible move, and it comes out by
deleting one line if NAT64 lands.

title: fix(data-products): /cluster/nextid does not reserve, so stop trusting it
body:
fix(data-products): /cluster/nextid does not reserve, so stop trusting it

Two resources created in the same second got the same vmid and the second
one died permanently:

    Failed to create LXC on sp1-sd-catalisatec-2: 500
    {"message":"CT 104 already exists on node 'sp1-sd-catalisatec-2'"}

getNextVmid() is a bare GET of Proxmox /cluster/nextid. That endpoint
answers with the lowest free id and does not reserve it, so concurrent
provisions all read the same number. The first POST won; the rest got the
500 above, it propagated out of the provisioner, and the resource was
marked failed with no retry on a fresh id. Seen live: three Flux clusters
created in the same second, all handed 104, one survived. Anyone clicking
create three times, or provisioning in batch, hit this.

The gap between reading an id and using it cannot be closed on the read
side — Proxmox has no reserving allocator to call. So it is closed on the
write side instead: createLxcWithFreshVmid makes allocation and creation
one retryable unit. It reads an id, tries to create, and on that specific
conflict throws the id away and reads a fresh one, up to five times. By
the time it asks again Proxmox has recorded the container that won, so the
next id is genuinely free.

Two details are deliberate. The retry fires only for a recognisable "that
id is taken" — anything else propagates untouched on the first attempt,
because retrying a real error would turn one legible failure into five,
hammer whatever is already broken, and bury the cause. And the config is
rebuilt per attempt, because Flux and Nexus derive the container's IP from
the vmid and Tide derives its egress NIC from it; a config built once
against the losing id would carry that id's address onto the winning
container, which on this cluster is the duplicate-IP failure mode that
takes hours to find.

The helper returns the vmid that actually took. Callers persist it as
lxcIds and roll back with it, so returning the first id read would leave
the platform stopping, exec'ing into, and eventually deleting somebody
else's container.

Adopted in the three provisioners the production smoke exercises — Tide,
Flux and Nexus. The other callers of getNextVmid (atlas, beacon, blaze,
email, herald, ignite, launch, spark, and the mesh runtime-adapter) are
left alone on purpose: they have the same defect, but nothing here can
exercise them, and refactoring what cannot be tested is how a race gets
traded for a regression. They are a follow-up.

Tests pin both halves of the contract: a create that collides once
succeeds on the next id, and a create that fails for any other reason is
attempted exactly once.

title: fix(flux,nexus): publish checks its result before marking active
body:
fix(flux,nexus): publish checks its result before marking active

`addPortForward` was made awaitable and result-returning on 2026-08-15
precisely so a failed port-forward would stop being invisible. Flux and
Nexus never got updated and kept calling it fire-and-forget, so the
provisioner marked the cluster `active`, stored an endpoint and emitted a
`success` event without ever knowing whether the host would forward
anything to the container.

What that costs a user is the worst shape a failure can take: not an
error, but a lie. They are told the cluster is ready, handed an address,
and the address refuses connections. Nothing in the UI, the event feed or
the status disagrees with the claim, so the time goes into doubting their
own client, their firewall and their credentials before anyone thinks to
check a NAT rule on the host. The failure is not hypothetical here — the
publish has lost the race for /run/xtables.lock against Docker, which is
why the iptables calls carry `-w 5` — and `addPortForward` resolves
`{ok:false}` rather than throwing, so nothing above it fails loudly on its
own. Inspecting the result is the only thing between a lost lock and a
customer holding a dead address.

Both call sites now await it and act on the outcome. A port that was not
published is not recorded on the cluster: the detail page renders its
connection panel from `endpoint` alone, without consulting status, so a
stored endpoint is a published one as far as the user is concerned. The
cluster goes `degraded` rather than `failed`, because the container is up
and the broker or engine is installed and running — only a host NAT rule
is missing. Tearing down working state over a contended lock would be a
worse outcome than an amber badge, and `degraded` is a live status for the
port-forward reconciler, so the rule is re-applied on the next pass and the
cluster can be repaired in place instead of rebuilt. The Herald event drops
to `partial` and carries prose naming the port, the underlying error and
the address the cluster would have had, so the operator can tell lock
contention (retry) from a broken rule (investigate) and can verify the
repair. Flux publishes its broker and RabbitMQ management forwards
independently: if only the management UI fails, the broker endpoint is
kept and the management port is withheld.

The new test drives both provisioners against a failing publish and
asserts on what was persisted, not on what a mock was called with. It
fails on the previous code — all five failure-path cases — while the two
happy-path controls keep passing, so it also pins that the fix does not
degrade clusters that are actually fine.

docs: the smoke found a third wall, and it is not code (#152)

The DNS fix (#151) worked in production: `apt-get update` now passes and
the Tide install runs on to the MinIO download, where it hits a different
wall.

    curl: (7) Failed to connect to dl.min.io port 443 after 2 ms:
          Could not connect to server

Two milliseconds is network-unreachable, not a timeout. Checked on the
host, `dl.min.io` is the one vendor host the platform downloads from that
has no AAAA record — deb.debian.org, github.com, registry-1.docker.io and
get.stalw.art all have real IPv6. Every Mesh pool here is IPv6-only, so a
Tide container cannot reach the only place it fetches MinIO from.

No code change reaches that host. It is mirror the binary somewhere
IPv6-reachable (Harbor is right there and this would be its first real
use), give the pool NAT64/DNS64, or install MinIO from somewhere else —
all owner decisions, so this is registered as C3 rather than attempted.

Also recorded: the trap that made this hard to see. `getent ahostsv6`
answers with an IPv4-mapped address (`::ffff:…`) when there is no AAAA at
all, which reads as "it has IPv6" to anyone skimming. The prefix is the
tell.

title: docs(plano): portal do parceiro — vitrine de tenants com marca do cliente
body:
docs(plano): portal do parceiro — vitrine de tenants com marca do cliente

Plano de execução para o portal onde o parceiro (primeiro: consultoria) cria e
acompanha os tenants Catalisa dos clientes dele — clientes que nunca vão
acessar o painel.

v1 é vitrine + duas ações: listar tenants, criar tenant, emitir token de
API. Todo o resto continua no painel.

O plano começa pelo que foi MEDIDO no código, não pelo que se supõe:

- `POST /auth/register` já cria IAM + org + usuário + billing, e já aceita
  um `ref` que hoje é um TODO logado — é o vínculo faltando, não um
  mecanismo novo;
- NÃO existe modelo de parceiro (`grep '^model (Partner|Reseller|
  Referral)'` = 0);
- sub-usuário NÃO é tenant: o dado dele pertence ao master, então os
  clientes do parceiro têm de ser masters-raiz — e nada os liga ao
  parceiro;
- token de API funciona de ponta a ponta (`Bearer tok_` → `ApiTokenStrategy`
  no guard global), então o mecanismo que a consultoria vai usar já existe;
- sem assinatura o painel não abre (o assistente toma a tela), então criar
  tenant SEM criar assinatura entrega cliente travado;
- `UserBranding` já tem a forma do whitelabel — reaproveitar, não inventar.

Cinco decisões justificadas (posse do tenant, quem entra no portal,
superfície mínima, o que o token significa, onde o portal mora), riscos com
mitigação, 6 fases com critério de pronto, e 5 questões abertas que
dependem do dono — a principal: o token precisa escrever ou só ler?

O default do tema é o NOSSO (os 125 semantic tokens do painel); o
whitelabel é sobreposição. Tokens resolvidos no `<head>`: tema aplicado
depois da montagem pisca roxo Catalisa antes de virar a marca do parceiro,
e numa demo isso é o cliente vendo a marca do fornecedor.

title: docs(consultorias): handoff da spec, e o plano do portal marcado como superado
body:
docs(consultorias): handoff da spec, e o plano do portal marcado como superado

Fecha a sessão de design de "Catalisa para consultorias": o cliente é dono do
próprio tenant e do CRM, e um terceiro opera para ele por concessão que ele
revoga.

A peça nova é UMA TABELA — `AccessGrant(grantor, grantee, resource, role)`,
plana, sem hierarquia. E a regra que a mantém barata: a concessão decide a
ENTRADA, nunca o filtro de consulta. Um tenant por vez, sempre. É isso que
deixa o custo em 1 guarda em vez de 33 módulos, porque todo serviço já
resolve o dono num lugar só.

O plano do portal (18/08) fica marcado como SUPERADO, com o motivo: apareceu
um requisito que muda tudo — o cliente final precisa do CRM. Se ele precisa
do CRM, precisa do painel, e um segundo aplicativo dividiria a atenção dele e
dobraria a manutenção. O painel ganha um modo, não um irmão. A árvore de
parceiros deu lugar à concessão, que custa MENOS e ainda expressa
co-atendimento.

O handoff registra o que quase sempre se perde entre sessões:

- o estado do código MEDIDO (o que existe: motor de metas, instalador de
  pacote, UserBranding, o seam de posse; o que não existe: rotina, rollup de
  objetivo, calendário de dias úteis, AccessGrant);
- as onze decisões com o que foi DESCARTADO junto — quem executa precisa
  saber as duas coisas;
- as regras de implementação que valem ouro: estender os testes de IDOR e
  nunca relaxar, negar por padrão em TODAS as rotas, reconferir na execução e
  não no enfileiramento, contexto na URL e cabeçalho na API;
- e o achado da consultoria que justifica o produto: a planilha compara mês parcial
  com mês inteiro e mostra 32% quando o ritmo real é 89%.

Nenhum código foi escrito, e não por falta de tempo: duas decisões precisam
vir antes. Revisão de segurança ANTES (isto é a reabertura controlada da
superfície que a auditoria acabou de fechar), e o que fazer com a ACL de rota
que está em 1 controller de 73 — uma camada de permissão que tem tela, grava
no banco e nenhum guard consulta.

title: docs(plano): portal do parceiro — vitrine de tenants com marca do cliente (#734)
body:
docs(plano): portal do parceiro — vitrine de tenants com marca do cliente (#734)

* docs(plano): portal do parceiro — vitrine de tenants com marca do cliente

Plano de execução para o portal onde o parceiro (primeiro: consultoria) cria e
acompanha os tenants Catalisa dos clientes dele — clientes que nunca vão
acessar o painel.

v1 é vitrine + duas ações: listar tenants, criar tenant, emitir token de
API. Todo o resto continua no painel.

O plano começa pelo que foi MEDIDO no código, não pelo que se supõe:

- `POST /auth/register` já cria IAM + org + usuário + billing, e já aceita
  um `ref` que hoje é um TODO logado — é o vínculo faltando, não um
  mecanismo novo;
- NÃO existe modelo de parceiro (`grep '^model (Partner|Reseller|
  Referral)'` = 0);
- sub-usuário NÃO é tenant: o dado dele pertence ao master, então os
  clientes do parceiro têm de ser masters-raiz — e nada os liga ao
  parceiro;
- token de API funciona de ponta a ponta (`Bearer tok_` → `ApiTokenStrategy`
  no guard global), então o mecanismo que a consultoria vai usar já existe;
- sem assinatura o painel não abre (o assistente toma a tela), então criar
  tenant SEM criar assinatura entrega cliente travado;
- `UserBranding` já tem a forma do whitelabel — reaproveitar, não inventar.

Cinco decisões justificadas (posse do tenant, quem entra no portal,
superfície mínima, o que o token significa, onde o portal mora), riscos com
mitigação, 6 fases com critério de pronto, e 5 questões abertas que
dependem do dono — a principal: o token precisa escrever ou só ler?

O default do tema é o NOSSO (os 125 semantic tokens do painel); o
whitelabel é sobreposição. Tokens resolvidos no `<head>`: tema aplicado
depois da montagem pisca roxo Catalisa antes de virar a marca do parceiro,
e numa demo isso é o cliente vendo a marca do fornecedor.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01NYVRNSQBR6K7LPmqe5EWzP

* docs(protótipo): sete telas navegáveis do portal do parceiro

O plano descrevia as telas; agora dá para vê-las. HTML estático, sem
nenhuma chamada de rede — abrir o arquivo basta.

Não é mock de aparência: cores, raios, sombras e tipografia foram copiados
de `apps/painel-cliente/src/theme/index.ts` sem alteração. É essa fidelidade
que faz o protótipo mostrar o que o whitelabel realmente troca — um punhado
de variáveis de marca — e o que ele não troca, que é a estrutura inteira.

O seletor de marca repinta a página ao vivo, e o de tema cobre os três
estados reais (claro, escuro, sistema), resolvidos no <head> antes da
primeira pintura — o mesmo requisito que o plano impõe ao portal de
verdade, porque tema aplicado depois da montagem pisca roxo Catalisa antes
de virar a marca do parceiro.

Três coisas que só apareceram ao desenhar:

- a vitrine consegue mostrar o risco do plano em vez de descrevê-lo: o
  cliente criado SEM assinatura ganha faixa de severidade na linha, e é
  exatamente o cliente que recebe um painel que não abre;
- a fronteira "o parceiro vê a ficha, não o conteúdo" vira conteúdo de
  tela — um cartão "O portal não mostra" na ficha, e os itens do painel
  apagados no rail. Esconder criaria a pergunta; mostrar apagado responde;
- o diálogo do token tem de dizer a verdade inteira: ele autentica COMO o
  cliente, logo enxerga o que a ficha esconde. Mostrar a fronteira na tela
  e entregar a chave que a atravessa em silêncio seria mentir por omissão.

O verde da consultoria é marcador de lugar — consultoria.com.br respondeu 403 à captura
automática — e o protótipo avisa isso na própria tela quando a marca do
parceiro está selecionada.

Verificado no navegador: as 7 telas, os 2 temas, as 2 marcas, sem erro de
console.

* docs(portal do parceiro): Q3 respondida — token de acesso total

Decisão do dono (18/08): o token é para tudo, escrita inclusive. Por ora a
consultoria só vai ler, mas a capacidade fica aberta desde o primeiro dia.

O que isso encerra: a v1 NÃO acrescenta escopo a `UserApiToken`, e a Fase 2
encolhe — era o único item do plano que dependia de trabalho de modelo
ainda não escrito.

O que isso move, e está registrado nos três lugares onde importa (§3 D4, a
tabela de riscos e a tela do token): o portal passa a emitir uma chave de
ESCRITA para um uso de LEITURA. As três guardas da emissão — escopo por
parceiro, auditoria de quem emitiu, nome e prazo obrigatórios — deixam de
ser boa prática e passam a ser o controle inteiro. Não há segundo muro
atrás delas, e o plano agora diz isso com essas palavras.

O que isso poupa, e é o argumento a favor: quando a escrita começar, nada
muda. Nenhuma migração, nenhum token reemitido, nenhuma janela de
indisponibilidade. Errar para o lado restritivo teria esse custo depois.

decisões pendentes do protótipo — não são mais nem uma coisa nem outra.

* docs(portal do parceiro): Q1/Q2/Q4/Q5 respondidas — parceiro vira árvore

As cinco questões do plano estão fechadas. Duas delas mudam arquitetura, não
só escopo.

Q2 — a consultoria cadastra parceiros abaixo dela, pelo portal. É a resposta que
mais mexe no plano, e não por causa da tela de cadastro, que é pequena: o
ESCOPO deixa de ser uma igualdade (`partnerId = eu`) e vira uma SUBÁRVORE.
Isso atravessa toda consulta, todo guarda e todo teste.

`parentId`. O Prisma 5 não faz CTE recursivo, então a relação sozinha
cairia em `$queryRaw` ou em N+1 de descida em JavaScript; com o caminho é um
`startsWith` indexado, uma consulta, sem SQL cru. Custa manter o caminho na
criação — e como a v1 não reparenta, ele nunca é reescrito.

E o risco que nasce junto: prefixo tem lado. `startsWith` invertido faz o
FILHO enxergar o PAI, em silêncio e com log limpo. Por isso a Fase 1 exige
três testes de escopo (irmão, filho, pai), não um.

Q4 — o parceiro edita a própria marca no portal. Duas escolhas mantêm isso
barato: logo por URL em vez de upload (quem busca a imagem é o navegador,
não o servidor, então não há pipeline de arquivo), e `customCss` FORA do
editor. O campo existe e o admin-panel já o injeta num <style>
(BrandedLayout.tsx:52); CSS arbitrário não roda JS, mas repinta a página e
dá para sobrepor um formulário falso ao de login. Num portal onde um
parceiro escreve o que roda no navegador do outro, isso não é tema, é
código.

Q1 — contadores agregados na ficha, sim; nenhum registro individual.
Q5 — `consultoria.catalisa.app` para a demo, e VAI MUDAR depois. Por isso
`domains` é lista, não campo único: na virada os dois endereços precisam
responder ao mesmo tempo, senão trocar de endereço vira indisponibilidade
agendada.

Estimativa: 5–6 → 6,5–8,5 sessões. O que cresceu foi a árvore, não a lista
de telas — e o corte barato, se precisar, é Fase 1.5 + 3.5: o modelo já
nasce em árvore e o cadastro de sub-parceiro fica conosco até o primeiro.

Protótipo vai de 7 para 9 telas, com as duas novas verificadas no navegador
(2 temas, 2 marcas, sem erro de console).

Sobrou uma pendência só, e não é decisão: a marca da consultoria, que o site não
entrega a fetch automatizado.

* docs(consultorias): handoff da spec, e o plano do portal marcado como superado

Fecha a sessão de design de "Catalisa para consultorias": o cliente é dono do
próprio tenant e do CRM, e um terceiro opera para ele por concessão que ele
revoga.

A peça nova é UMA TABELA — `AccessGrant(grantor, grantee, resource, role)`,
plana, sem hierarquia. E a regra que a mantém barata: a concessão decide a
ENTRADA, nunca o filtro de consulta. Um tenant por vez, sempre. É isso que
deixa o custo em 1 guarda em vez de 33 módulos, porque todo serviço já
resolve o dono num lugar só.

O plano do portal (18/08) fica marcado como SUPERADO, com o motivo: apareceu
um requisito que muda tudo — o cliente final precisa do CRM. Se ele precisa
do CRM, precisa do painel, e um segundo aplicativo dividiria a atenção dele e
dobraria a manutenção. O painel ganha um modo, não um irmão. A árvore de
parceiros deu lugar à concessão, que custa MENOS e ainda expressa
co-atendimento.

O handoff registra o que quase sempre se perde entre sessões:

- o estado do código MEDIDO (o que existe: motor de metas, instalador de
  pacote, UserBranding, o seam de posse; o que não existe: rotina, rollup de
  objetivo, calendário de dias úteis, AccessGrant);
- as onze decisões com o que foi DESCARTADO junto — quem executa precisa
  saber as duas coisas;
- as regras de implementação que valem ouro: estender os testes de IDOR e
  nunca relaxar, negar por padrão em TODAS as rotas, reconferir na execução e
  não no enfileiramento, contexto na URL e cabeçalho na API;
- e o achado da consultoria que justifica o produto: a planilha compara mês parcial
  com mês inteiro e mostra 32% quando o ritmo real é 89%.

Nenhum código foi escrito, e não por falta de tempo: duas decisões precisam
vir antes. Revisão de segurança ANTES (isto é a reabertura controlada da
superfície que a auditoria acabou de fechar), e o que fazer com a ACL de rota
que está em 1 controller de 73 — uma camada de permissão que tem tela, grava
no banco e nenhum guard consulta.

title: fix(security): frescor anti-replay BB (F-9) + sanitiza customFields da captura (F-15) + TLS do BB Storage seguro (F-11)
body:
fix(security): frescor anti-replay BB (F-9) + sanitiza customFields da captura (F-15) + TLS do BB Storage seguro (F-11)

F-9: bb-events já era timing-safe (C-7); faltava a janela de frescor. assertFreshWebhook
rejeita request assinado porém com timestamp fora da janela (replay). Fail-OPEN se o
timestamp não parsear (a assinatura já impede forja) — não quebra ingestão BB. Janela
via BB_WEBHOOK_FRESHNESS_SEC (300s). Spec passou a usar timestamp fresco (FRESH_TS).

F-15: submitLead cappa/coage customFields (máx 30 chaves, 64 chars/chave, 2000/valor,
tudo string) antes de entrar no customData → reduz poluição de CRM e limita payload de
prompt-injection no agente do tenant. NÃO adiciona captcha (não muda conversão).

F-11: cert do BB Storage VALIDA (verificado ao vivo, ssl_verify_result=0), então
rejectUnauthorized:false era desnecessário e desligava a autenticação do canal. Agora
secure-by-default (1 https.Agent compartilhado), com escape CATALISA_STORAGE_INSECURE_TLS=true.

tsc limpo nos 4; capture-links spec 5/5. bb-events spec não roda local (módulo trava o
jest, desligado no CI) — validação por tsc + smoke ao vivo.

title: feat(consultorias): endpoints de concessão e auditoria de acesso (E6)
body:
feat(consultorias): endpoints de concessão e auditoria de acesso (E6)

As telas "Meus acessos" e "Conceder acesso" do lado do dono, mais o histórico.

`GET /access-grants` (concedidos), `GET /access-grants/received` (recebidos),
`POST /access-grants`, `DELETE /access-grants/:id`, `GET /access-grants/log`.

O DTO NÃO tem `grantorId`, de propósito: o dono sai sempre do usuário
autenticado resolvido pelo seam, nunca do corpo. Escopo derivado de parâmetro
é a família de defeito que a auditoria encontrou quatro vezes nesta base — um
campo `grantorId` deixaria qualquer pessoa conceder acesso à empresa de outra.
Todo campo usado está declarado, porque o ValidationPipe roda com
`whitelist: true` e descarta em silêncio o que não estiver no DTO, devolvendo
200 e gravando sem o campo.

Este controller inteiro é indelegável — dentro de um contexto de atuação
responde 403, porque o convidado ampliaria a própria chave. A regra fica na
guarda, não aqui: uma segunda lista divergiria da primeira, e a esquecida
seria a que vale. A catraca do inventário confirmou sozinha, pegando as 4
rotas novas e exigindo decisão.

`AccessLogService.record` NUNCA derruba a requisição. Auditoria que quebra a
operação transforma problema de observabilidade em indisponibilidade, e o
primeiro reflexo de quem for consertar seria desligar o log — perdendo o que
ele protege.

O histórico devolve os dois lados (o que fizeram na minha empresa E o que a
minha fez fora). Um dono que só visse o primeiro não conseguiria auditar a
própria equipe operando em cliente.

"Empresa não existe" e "é sub-usuário" recebem a mesma mensagem: senão a tela
de conceder vira verificador de quem tem conta na plataforma.

42 suítes / 557 testes verdes. check:di 741 classes, 0 problemas.

title: feat(consultorias): inventário de rotas para a baseline de negação (E0)
body:
feat(consultorias): inventário de rotas para a baseline de negação (E0)

Varredura estática dos 73 controllers do painel: 577 rotas, com método,
caminho completo, handler e se a rota é @Public. A suíte de negação da
Fase 1 precisa cobrir TODA rota, não uma amostra — amostra é o que deixa
um controller esquecido continuar esquecido. Não há Swagger em main.ts
para ler a tabela de rotas, e subir o Nest para andar no router exige
banco, então o inventário sai dos próprios decorators.

O script confere o próprio total contra uma contagem independente e falha
se divergirem. A primeira versão reportou 559 rotas — número limpo,
plausível e errado: um `@ApiOperation({...})` multilinha limpava o bloco
de decorators e levava o `@Get` de cima junto, sumindo com três
controllers inteiros. Num inventário que alimenta suíte de negação, isso
é rota que nunca é chamada parecendo coberta.

`--check` reprova quando alguém acrescenta rota sem caso de negação.

feat(consultorias): guarda central e contexto de atuação (E3)

A peça que faz a concessão valer. Um guarda, não 33 módulos.

A concessão decide a ENTRADA, nunca o filtro: confirmada a chave, tudo roda
como o dono daquele tenant, exatamente como hoje. O caminho oposto — listagem
devolvendo "o meu mais o compartilhado" — exigiria consultar permissão dentro
de cada consulta do sistema e transformaria todo defeito de escopo em
vazamento entre empresas.

Como o dono efetivo troca: `AsyncLocalStorage`, lido dentro de
`resolveRootMasterId` e `getVisibleUserIds` — os DOIS únicos pontos.
Descartados: provider REQUEST-scoped (o escopo sobe por todo o grafo de DI,
com risco direto no check:di) e passar o tenant por parâmetro (114 call sites
e 73 controllers, cada esquecimento virando vazamento).

Middleware + guarda, e não só guarda: é restrição real do Nest, não estilo.
Middleware tem `next()` e embrulha a requisição inteira no `run()`, mas roda
antes da autenticação e não sabe quem é o usuário. A guarda sabe, mas não tem
`next` — um `run()` dentro dela fecharia o escopo ao retornar, e o handler
executaria FORA do contexto, lendo o tenant de quem opera enquanto a barra
diz que se está dentro do cliente. Então o middleware abre um porta-contexto
vazio (que não autoriza nada) e a guarda preenche por referência, já dentro.
Guarda sem escopo estoura 500 em vez de seguir — seguir seria o pior caso.

A sutileza que decide se protege ou vaza: a substituição só vale quando o id
sendo resolvido é o do PRÓPRIO ator. `getRootMasterId` também é chamado com
ids de terceiros (validar responsável, resolver dono de lead alheio), e trocar
nesses casos afirmaria que uma pessoa qualquer pertence ao tenant do cliente.

O que a guarda NUNCA troca: a identidade do ator, o registro de auditoria e a
lista de indelegáveis. Operador agindo dentro de um cliente continua sendo,
para log e bloqueio, a pessoa da consultoria.

Negar é o padrão: sem cabeçalho roda como sempre; com cabeçalho e sem
concessão viva, 403 — não lista vazia, que faria o operador achar que o
cliente não tem dado. Empresa inexistente e empresa que não concedeu recebem
a MESMA resposta, senão o cabeçalho vira verificador de existência.

As sete indelegáveis numa lista só, com um teste cada. A API não tem uma
segunda — se tivesse, as duas divergiriam e a esquecida seria a que vale.
Casam por SEGMENTO, não por prefixo de string: `startsWith` faria
`/users-report` cair na regra de `/users`.

Delegáveis na Fase 1: GOALS, PIPELINE, LEAD_TYPES — os únicos cujos caminhos
de posse provadamente passam pelo seam. Conceder fora disso é NEGADO com
motivo; aceitar e não fazer efeito seria pior, porque o dono veria na tela uma
concessão que não protege nada.

Testado o que o desenho assume e ninguém confere: o contexto sobrevive à
cadeia assíncrona, NÃO vaza entre requisições concorrentes, e NÃO atravessa a
fronteira de uma fila (job enfileirado dentro do contexto e executado depois
não herda a atuação — entre enfileirar e executar a concessão pode ter sido
revogada).

test(consultorias): paga a dívida da E0 — baseline de negação em todas as rotas

A §5.1 pedia uma baseline congelada de dois tenants. Eu tinha entregue o
inventário e as catracas, provado o ciclo por smoke manual, e DECLARADO isso
como dívida. Isto fecha.

10 asserções sobre as 582 rotas do inventário, não sobre amostra:

  · sem concessão nenhuma, TODA rota guardada é negada
  · com todos os recursos concedidos, SÓ as mapeadas passam
    (o par do anterior — uma guarda que negasse tudo passaria lá e falharia cá)
  · concessão de um recurso não abre os outros
  · VIEW não escreve, em nenhuma rota
  · SEM cabeçalho, nada é bloqueado — o modo próprio é o de sempre
  · agir na própria empresa não abre contexto nem vira linha de auditoria
  · empresa inexistente e empresa que não concedeu: mesma resposta
  · a auditoria registra com o OPERADOR como ator

Roda no nível da guarda, sem banco. O caminho HTTP já foi provado uma vez com
API e Postgres reais; isso responde "funciona?". Não responde "continua
funcionando no próximo commit?" — para isso precisa rodar em qualquer máquina
e no CI. As duas são necessárias.

VERIFICADO QUE MORDE, sabotando a guarda de propósito:
  · fazer rota não mapeada passar        → reprova
  · remover o corte `grants.size === 0`  → NÃO reprovava

O segundo caso ensinou algo: aquele corte é redundante para o ACESSO (a rota
mapeada nega depois, por recurso). Não é redundante para a MENSAGEM — é o que
distingue "esta empresa não te conhece" de "você tem acesso aqui, mas não a
esta área". Acrescentei a asserção que faltava, e agora a sabotagem reprova.

Dois detalhes de teste que valem registro:
  · os specs declaram `GrantResource`/`GrantRole` e sobrepõem `@prisma/client`,
    como `leads.service.spec.ts` já faz com `UserRole`. Catraca que só roda
    onde o client foi gerado é catraca que não roda no CI.
  · `attempt(guard, route, undefined)` acionava o valor PADRÃO do parâmetro —
    o teste "sem cabeçalho" estava mandando o cabeçalho. Agora é `null`.

feat(consultorias): auditoria da atuação na guarda, e a prova do critério (E8)

A guarda passa a gravar `AccessLog` quando alguém age dentro de outro tenant.
Faltava, e era o rastro que a especificação diz não existir em lugar nenhum se
não for gravado aqui: quando o painel chama o Building Blocks, ele usa a
credencial do próprio cliente, então o log do BB dirá "a conta do cliente
enviou" e é estruturalmente incapaz de distinguir o operador.

Toda ESCRITA vira linha, sempre. Leitura não: uma tela de funil dispara
dezenas de GET por minuto, e gravar todos afogaria o histórico exatamente no
que ele existe para mostrar. Leitura registra só a ENTRADA, no máximo uma vez
por janela de 10 min — em memória e por processo, porque perder um ENTER por
restart repete a linha (barato) e o que não pode faltar é escrita, que não
passa por esse caminho.

=== SMOKE CONTRA API REAL, DOIS TENANTS, POSTGRES REAL ===

Critério de pronto da Fase 1, verificado ponta a ponta:

  1. operador sem concessão                    → 403
  2. dono concede PIPELINE/EDIT                → 201
  3. operador entra e trabalha                 → 200, com eco do cabeçalho
  4. dono revoga                               → 200
  5. PRÓXIMA requisição do operador            → 403
     e só do recurso revogado — PIPELINE segue → 200

A prova que importa mais: dentro do contexto, `GET /lead-types` devolve
`CLIENTE_DO_DONO` e NÃO `CLIENTE_DA_consultoria`. O operador enxerga o dado do
cliente, não o próprio — é a troca do seam funcionando de verdade, e é
exatamente o que a normalização da E1-bis tornou possível.

Também verificado ao vivo:
  · concessão de PIPELINE não abre LEAD_TYPES  → 403 (granularidade real)
  · concessão VIEW bloqueia escrita            → 403
  · ler credencial em contexto                 → 403 (indelegável 1)
  · criar webhook de saída em contexto         → 403 (indelegável 2)
  · rota não mapeada (/workflows) em contexto  → 403 (omissão fecha)
  · trocar o tenant na URL para quem não concedeu → 403
  · AccessLog com ENTER e POST /leads, ator = o operador

Um susto no caminho, que vale registrar: o processo antigo da API não morria
com `pkill`, o novo falhava em silêncio e o `/health` respondia do VELHO. Por
vinte minutos eu estava testando código sem a auditoria e concluindo que ela
não funcionava. Verificação de deploy que confia em health check responde
"está no ar", nunca "está no ar com o SEU código".

body:
refactor(tenancy): uma única resolução de dono, com catraca (E1-bis)

A especificação afirmava, e o handoff repetia, que "todo serviço do painel
resolve o dono num lugar só". Medido: falso. Havia duas implementações da
mesma CTE recursiva — `TenantHierarchyService.getRootMasterId` e uma cópia
literal em `lead-types/lead-type-scope.ts`, com comentário admitindo a
réplica — mais pontos que pulavam as duas.

Por que ninguém percebeu: para um master, `resolveRootMasterId(id) === id`.
Enquanto o dono é sempre o autenticado, `{ ownerId: userId }` e o seam
devolvem exatamente o mesmo valor. As formas são indistinguíveis, e todo
teste existente passa nas duas.

Elas divergem no instante em que uma concessão de acesso troca o dono
efetivo — e divergem em SILÊNCIO: a barra de contexto diz "operando em
Fulano" e a consulta lê os leads de quem opera. É o modo de falha que a
própria spec nomeia, "operar no cliente errado", chegando pela porta que
ninguém vigiava.

O que muda:

- `shared/tenancy/root-master.ts` passa a ser a implementação canônica;
  `TenantHierarchyService` vira casca fina sobre ela e `lead-type-scope`
  reexporta, então os 7 call sites não mudam.
- `leads.getOwnerIdForLead` perde o curto-circuito
  `if (!creator.parentId) return creatorId`, que disparava JUSTAMENTE no
  caso do master — o caminho mais comum nunca passava pelo seam. De quebra,
  some uma consulta por criação de lead.
- `leads.findAll` e `getStatsByStatus` passam a escopar pelo seam em vez de
  ler `parentId` na mão. Recebem o usuário já carregado, para não fazer a
  mesma consulta duas vezes.
- `buildBulkScopeWhere` idem. NÃO foi unificado com o resto porque diverge
  de verdade para PANEL_ADMIN (`{}` contra `{ ownerId }`) — unificar seria
  mudança de comportamento disfarçada de refatoração.
- Catraca `no-duplicate-tenant-cte.spec.ts`: reprova uma terceira cópia,
  varrendo API e worker (a guarda irmã esqueceu o worker e pagou no deploy).

Sobre o spec de leads: 3 mudanças, nenhuma asserção enfraquecida. O mock de
`getRootMasterId` devolvia um id fixo para QUALQUER entrada — ficção que
nunca aparecia porque o curto-circuito impedia a chamada. Tornado fiel à
hierarquia das fixtures. E `clearAllMocks` não drena a fila de
`mockResolvedValueOnce`: com uma consulta a menos, a sobra vazava para o
teste seguinte e a falha aparecia longe da causa.

Comportamento nulo, medido: 40 suítes / 528 testes verdes; a linha de base
era 39 / 525, e o delta é exatamente a catraca nova.

feat(consultorias): seletor, barra de contexto e tela de Acessos (E7)

O lado do dono e a entrada do operador.

Tela `Acessos` (`/settings/acessos`): quem tem chave da minha empresa, para
quê, até quando — e o botão de revogar. Esta tela é o que transforma a
concessão de CONVENIÊNCIA em CONSENTIMENTO: se o operador cria o tenant, é
ele quem se auto-concede, e sem esta tela o dono nunca saberia. É também o que
sustenta a conversa de proteção de dados — o cliente é controlador do dado
dele e delegou de forma registrada e reversível.

O cabeçalho de atuação entra no ÚNICO request interceptor do axios. São ~50
módulos `*Api.ts`; pedir que cada um lembre garantiria que algum esqueceria, e
cabeçalho esquecido falha em silêncio — a chamada acerta a PRÓPRIA conta
enquanto a tela afirma que se está dentro do cliente.

DEFEITO CORRIGIDO junto: `api.get` deduplica GETs concorrentes por URL. Sem o
contexto na chave, `GET /leads` na empresa A e na empresa B colidiriam — a
segunda reusaria a promessa em voo da primeira e receberia os leads do cliente
errado, sem erro nenhum.

Barra de contexto acima do cabeçalho, não dentro: o operador precisa ver em
qual empresa está antes de ler qualquer outra coisa. Cor de sinal (não a da
marca, que o olho filtra) e saída sempre visível. Some sozinha no modo próprio.

DESVIO REGISTRADO, para decisão do dono: a especificação (D10) pede o contexto
como PREFIXO de caminho (`/c/<empresa>/metas`). Aqui é parâmetro de consulta
(`?c=<empresa>`). Preserva integralmente a propriedade que motivou a decisão —
cada aba inequívoca, botão voltar funcionando, link compartilhável, nenhuma
contaminação entre abas — sem duplicar a árvore inteira de rotas do App.tsx,
que tem 418 linhas lidas por regex pelo `screenScan`. Trocar depois é mudança

front não roda no CI.

body:
refactor(auth)!: remove a ACL de rota morta, substituída pelo AccessGrant (E1)

O `@RequireRoute` existia em 1 controller de 73. O PermissionGuard estava
registrado como APP_GUARD global mas só nega quando a rota tem o
decorator — ou seja, passava direto em 72 controllers. Havia tela de
permissões gravando linhas que nenhum guard lia, e uma auditoria já
apontou isso como achado sistêmico.

Ligar a concessão de acesso por cima disso deixaria o sistema com dois
modelos de autorização, um deles enfeite — e decoração que PARECE
proteger é pior que ausência, porque gera confiança. Decisão do dono:
remover e declarar substituída.

O que sai: decorator, guard (+spec), o módulo routes/, os 15 usos, os 4
endpoints que só alimentavam a tabela, os métodos setPermissions/
getAvailableRoutes/getUserPermissions, a tela e o cliente do front, e os
modelos Permission/Route.

Modelo de dados da concessão entre tenants. Só o dado — a guarda que o
consome é a E3.

`AccessGrant(grantor, grantee, resource, role)`, plana, sem hierarquia.
Descartada a árvore de parceiros: mais tabelas, escopo tudo-ou-nada, o
operador acima do cliente por construção, e uma classe de defeito própria
(prefixo invertido faz filho enxergar pai).

Decisões que estão no schema e merecem estar aqui:

- `@@unique([grantorId, granteeId, resource])` — um par tem no máximo uma
  linha por recurso. Duas linhas conflitantes deixariam a pergunta "o que
  autoriza esta chamada?" sem resposta única.
- Revogação é `revokedAt`, não DELETE: apagar a linha apagaria junto a prova
  de que o acesso existiu, que é o que a auditoria precisa manter.
- `AccessLog` sem chave estrangeira, de propósito — registro de auditoria
  precisa sobreviver à exclusão do usuário e do tenant que descreve.
  Integridade referencial aqui apagaria a prova junto com o ator.
- `AccessLog.action` é texto, não enum: a lista cresce com o produto e um
  enum obrigaria migração para registrar ação nova.
- Três relações distintas em User (concede / recebe / autorizou), porque o
  tenant dono e a pessoa que clicou são coisas diferentes e a auditoria
  precisa dos dois.

O `GrantResource` traz os 10 recursos do catálogo, mas estar no enum NÃO é
ser delegável: a Fase 1 aceita concessão só em GOALS, PIPELINE e LEAD_TYPES,
os únicos cujos caminhos de posse provadamente passam pelo seam. Os demais
esbarram em eixos que a concessão não move — o tenantId do runtime de
workflow, o OrganizationMember do billing e o JWT do BB. A lista de

title: docs: the C findings became fixes, and one new one took their place (#176)
body:
docs: the C findings became fixes, and one new one took their place (#176)

C10, C11 and C12 are closed by #173-#175. What is worth carrying forward
is not that they are closed but what closing them turned up.

Atlas revocation chose NOLOGIN over DROP ROLE because issuance grants the
role CREATE ON SCHEMA public, so the first object it creates makes DROP
fail — and a drop that commonly fails is a revocation that commonly
leaves the access running. Open sessions are terminated after the
NOLOGIN, not before, or the pooler reconnects and it merely looks like it
worked. On the way there: the store keeps the raw username while issuance
writes it unquoted, which Postgres folds to lower case, so without one
shared helper revocation would have altered a role that does not exist
and reported success against nothing.

The Courier decision is the one to remember. Adding it to
PRODUCT_DESCRIPTORS would have been inert rather than merely wrong:
collectForProduct pushes to unresolved and continues before extraForwards
is ever consulted, so the entry would sit in the list looking like
coverage while emitting zero rules. Port 4190, the live ManageSieve rule
that was one removeOrphans=true from deletion, now has an owner.

One new finding replaces them: the JSON store has no read-modify-write
atomicity, so concurrent writers lose updates. Production runs Postgres,
but the code default is json — the same shape as the crypto ceiling.

Three questions are left explicitly for the owner, including whether
MAIL_PORTS omitting 143 is deliberate.

title: chore(backup): survey the backup surface, and put the Spark scheduler where it lives (#177)
body:
chore(backup): survey the backup surface, and put the Spark scheduler where it lives (#177)

Answering a direct question — are the backup and snapshot features reusing
each other, or duplicating and overlapping? The full map is in
docs/backup-surface-survey.md. The short version is that there is much less
overlap than the word count suggests, and the real defect is not duplication
at all.

Five surfaces use the word "backup". Spark is the only one that takes data,
moves it somewhere else and can put it back: BGSAVE inside the primary LXC,
poll INFO persistence, mc cp the RDB up to a Tide provisioned for that cluster
alone, and the same path backwards for restore. Forge has two thin wrappers
over Proxmox's own endpoints — vzdump jobs at /backup, and qemu/lxc snapshots,
the latter already written once and shared correctly between the VM and CT
pages. Atlas has no backups and says so in a 501, with the AtlasBackup type and
its table deliberately left as scaffolding; that is not dead code and should
not be deleted. Tide, Flux, Nexus, Blaze, Herald and Ignite have nothing.

So the tempting unification is the one to refuse. A vzdump is the hypervisor
archiving a whole guest; a BGSAVE is Valkey forking and writing its own dataset
while still serving; a qemu snapshot is a point-in-time on the storage layer.
The word "snapshot" alone means two different things inside the same directory
— a vzdump *mode* in run-backup-dialog, and the *thing being created* in
create-snapshot-dialog. An interface over all three would have to lie about at
least two of them.

What was genuinely duplicated, and is fixed here, is small: the two vzdump
dialogs each carried their own hand-written list of the same three parameters,
and had already drifted — compression read "ZSTD (recommended)" when you
scheduled a backup and plain "ZSTD" when you ran one now. One copy now, in
lib/vzdump-options.ts, whose header also records the larger problem that
deduplication does not fix: those three storages are the mock server's, not the
cluster's, so on real hardware two of them do not exist and the third is the
small root-backed pool storage-defaults exists to avoid. That is a live fix to
what the product offers rather than a dedup, so it is written up, not done.

The thing worth the survey is data-products/backup-scheduler.ts, which is moved
to spark/. It was filed in the shared-leaf directory beside dns.ts,
default-node.ts and quota.ts — files that exist because several modules needed
the same answer — while importing SparkCluster, hardcoding memcached and
calling spark/service's runBackup. Nothing else in the product has a backup
implementation for it to have served. The cost is not tidiness: it made the
file look deletable. This work began with it already flagged as dead, which
follows honestly from grepping src/ for its name, because its one real caller
is instrumentation.ts — outside src/, run by Next at server boot. Deleting it
would have broken nothing observable. No route fails, no test fails, tsc stays
green, and scheduled Spark backups just stop, with lastBackupAt quietly ageing
on every cluster until someone needs a restore. That is the same failure the
fake Atlas backups had: the screen keeps saying the data is protected.

It now sits beside the store and service it drives, with a header explaining
what nearly happened, and instrumentation.ts names Spark in its import.

Ranked next, with effort and risk, in the survey: the storage picker that
offers storages that only exist in the mock; Atlas's green "WAL on" badge for a
flag nothing reads; BackupApi implemented twice across core and forge, where
the copy sdk actually uses inlines its paths instead of reading API_PATHS; and
fmtDate, five byte-identical copies, ranked last precisely because it is the
easiest and the least reviewable.

Verified: typecheck clean, spark and data-products suites pass (76 and 95),
web build succeeds, no new lint findings in any touched file.
